utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, would you like to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. We are still on paragraph 4.1 of the indictment. I have dealt with the allegations concerning paragraph 11, which fit in within the time frame of 4.1 and I have made my observations on those matters to the Court. Looking still then at paragraph 4.1, there is the further allegation of a beating of a number of Muslim males seized and detained at Prijedor military barracks. One observation we have to make about this is that it is outside that time frame of 24th to 27th May that heads off this section of paragraph 4.1 but, no doubt, those allegations fit elsewhere within the framework of this case. Again, if I may make this observation, that there are two witnesses alone who give evidence of beatings at Prijedor barracks, Uzeir Besic and Sead Halvadzic. The allegation concerning Uzeir Besic is on 3rd June 1992 and amounts after his beating in the corridor of the barracks to a man he says was Dusko Tadic giving him a kicking whilst he was on the ground after his interrogation. Again, we have made observations about how people are able to make these allegations and this kind of sighting, and we emphasise that the Court will have to consider carefully whether this is just one more allegation thrown into the pot or happened. There does not seem to be in the context of this case much other evidence that links Dusko Tadic with Prijedor barracks. Our submission is that it is highly isolated and we would say something that the Court should treat with extreme caution, particularly when one considers the evidence of the second witness, Sead Halvadzic, who was there on 8th June 1992 having been taken captive. This was one of the identification witnesses who had not known Dusko Tadic before. His identification of the defendant using the photospread on, I believe, 14th June 1996, over four years later, a black and white photograph, having resided in a country where the newspaper that he claimed to have only looked at, [redacted] we know from the media expert, Thomas Deichmann, who gave evidence, had printed some 82 articles between February 1994 and October 1996 containing information about Dusko Tadic. He had the peculiar observation about his desire to hunt down war criminals, wherever they were. Interestingly as well, within his evidence all his allegations concerning his own beating and indeed people he came across, if I can put it this way, refer to all the big names in Omarska -- Meakic and others. We submit to the Court that his evidence should be taken with extreme caution, particularly in view of some four years later using the photospread as a means of identification in circumstances when there had been a great deal of publicity about this case throughout the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, what did you say, that he claimed to have only looked at [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That paper was then examined, was it ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: --- as to its contents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, it is the biggest newspaper in [redacted] Thomas Deichmann told us, and it contained 82 articles in that period of time. One has to make this kind of observation, people may not want to look at this kind of content having experienced these horrific circumstances, but the fact of the matter is when one walks past newsstands, when one switches on the television, when one casually sees a newspaper within a doctor's waiting room, these photographs are there and in a way it is difficult to avoid. Perhaps it affects the subconscious of this kind of witness to put it in his memory bank, so to speak, so that when that photospread is laid before him there is something there that triggers a recollection. One has to be wary of this, particularly when a gap of four years has existed between what amounts to a fairly brief confrontation to a process of identification. Again, it is significant, we would submit, that in his evidence he said that the name "Tadic" was being used, the surname of the defendant. Quite why people would express themselves in that way and in those circumstances is slightly odd to imagine; quite why the name should be used at all is difficult to conceive. But there we are. He said he did not know this man, and claimed an identification many years later through what, we would say, is a flawed process by them. Moving from paragraph 4.1, because paragraph 12 which is referred to within that section of the indictment exists as a separate substantive count, and I will address the Court about that at the end of the addresses relating to those substantive counts on the indictment. Therefore, at this stage, I turn now to paragraph 4.2 of the indictment which principally contains the allegations that are contained within the substantive evidence, but at this stage it is appropriate to look at the sightings of Dusko Tadic on numerous occasions in the three main camps within opstina Prijedor as the opening remarks of paragraph 4.2 of the indictment set out. I have made observations about sightings, but we say it is significant here to consider the wide variety of uniforms and, indeed, facial descriptions that have formed so much a feature of this case. If an analysis of the evidence is undertaken, in a period of some four days, 14th June to 18th June, the wide variety of facial descriptions of the man alleged to be Dusko Tadic is extraordinary. It ranges from having a beard of 15 days to one month, as said by the witness Sakib Sivac ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Kay, do you have transcript cites readily available as you are referring us to this evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not have that on this particular material here. I am sure it could be made available to the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have the transcripts and so we can locate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It ranges also on 14th June to an unkempt beard; the 16th June, 10 days's growth as described by Edin Mrkalj; a few days growth on 17th June as described by Emir Beganovic; a beard as described on 18th June by Elvir Grozdanic; also on 18th June, Armin Mujcic, two days unshaven. The wide variety of facial appearance in that short period of time and, indeed, spanning throughout the whole history of these events from May to August and even on to October 1992, we say, throws into this evidence distinct reasons why the Court should be cautious and careful about the alleged sightings of the accused. Of course, people may make a mistake and describe someone as being unshaven and having a beard, but the alarming feature of 15 days to one month growth, to being unshaven to a few days growth, shows such a variation that, in our submission, this defendant is entitled to have this evidence considered with great caution. Uniforms are the same. Your Honour, Judge McDonald referred yesterday to Professor Wagenaar's remarks on military uniforms. We are not talking here about whether they are huzzars or guards, Coldstream Guards. We are not talking here about distinguishing between old army uniforms or new army uniforms where people may have a picture of a soldier at the back of their mind. We are talking here about clothing that does not derive from any military stores department. We are talking here about people being dressed in different clothing, almost as similar to people wearing civilian clothes differently. It is a wide variety of clothing. We say that is significant for this defendant, because it is out of that uniform category into clothing generally. Again when one considers the wardrobe that he should have had from May until even August, it is so different and so varied even on the same day that there again is great need for caution about the allegations concerning this defendant and the reliability of the evidence concerned. Again, just taking that period of 14th to 16th June, on 14th June a new camouflage uniform with handcuffs on the belt as described by Sakib Sivac; on 14th June camouflage uniform as described by Draguna Jaskic. Zemka Sahbaz describes coffee and pale or dark green and dark coffee with a hat like a shield with a brim. Senija Elkasovic describes coffee and paler or greenish and white coffee. Witness S, in mid June, a camo police top; on 16th June, Edin Mrkalj, a blue police jacket. We have other occasions where he is described as wearing a headband, a civilian suit that we discussed yesterday that was like a camouflage uniform, with a white belt, without a white belt, with sunglasses, with a cap with a kokarda, with a giraffe jacket, in a black pilot's jacket and trousers and headband, in June, as described by Dzemal Deomic, and blue jeans and a dark blue t-shirt, as described by Hasiba Harambasic. This wide variety, we say, should cause this Court to have caution about this evidence because the defence here is that this defendant was not there at that time and it is the defence of alibi. We ask the Court in their investigation of these matters to bear these features very much in mind when one looks at the accuracy of these allegations. When one considers sightings in the camps, perhaps Omarska is the best example to take, there are a number of brief sightings, as I would put them, as described by Hamdija Kahrimanovic, Sejad Jakupovic, Kemal Susic, Uzeir Besic, Husein Hodzic, Nihad Haskic and Saud Hrnic. I have not included within that the paragraph 6 witnesses. Then you have other witnesses where there are circumstances about the identification that we say should cause this Court to apply that caution we have asked. The witness Dzemal Deomic being held in that garage around the corner of the administration building in June 1992, this was the witness who had the photograph put in front of him, because he claimed he had seen Dusko Tadic arriving in a black pilot's jacket with a headband on a motor bike. This witness was convinced of this sighting. It became clear in cross-examination that he was actually using the photograph believing it was a photograph of that particular time that he was there, and justifying this sighting by reference to the van in the photograph that had been taken in February 1996 and the puddle in the photograph, justifying his memory by, "Oh, it had rained on that day that I saw him", as though this was an image before this witness that justified this occasion when that photograph was taken a long while later, in February 1996, and not when he was there in June 1992. It indicates to us the power of suggestibility of witnesses who have been through this ghastly circumstance and ghastly period within Omarska. It is tragic almost. It is something that we have to bring to the Court's attention and with respect to that poor victim, but it was there for all to see that this was being justified in a way that was absolutely impossible. We have other sightings such as made also by this witness in rooms of the White House where at one time there were 150 people in this small room at the back right-hand side of the White House. He was in the far right corner, and in circumstances which cannot have been of the easiest nor the best claiming a sighting of Dusko Tadic. In a way, many of the circumstances in which these witnesses were held and the massive grouping of all these people are something that the Court, we say, should have in mind in relation to the accuracy of a number of those sightings. There was the witness Kasim Mesic. He was there when the man Kera who appeared, unfortunately, to have gone mad and lost his senses and was shot by a guard on the pista when he asked for more bread. He had been a witness who was stealing glances sideways, lying down. We had cross-examination concerning the flower tubs that boarded the pista on each side and between which the men on that place were being held. In those circumstances, his identification of the defendant again four years later in June 1996 using the procedure of the photospread, we say, should cause great concern about the reliability of such evidence. It is a problem for the Prosecution in producing evidence in that form with that degree of delay before a witness is put through appropriate procedures. Interestingly enough, the next witness who followed Kasim Mesic was a man called Witness R and, for no apparent reason, he told us that there was no problem with the flower tubs. Quite why one witness following another should have had that mind, we say perhaps is beyond coincidence and for some reason he had been compelled to bring that to our attention. Another sighting, which is connected to a beating, comes through the witness of Mehmedalija Huskic. This is a significant witness and one that we say gives great credence to our submission of the way witnesses will, perhaps, allege sightings against this kind of defendant before this Tribunal. He was in the electrical workshop on 20th June 1992, two days after the infamous events within the hangar. We know how many people were in that electrical workshop, and many of them make up the witnesses in relation to paragraph 6. What he alleges on that day was that Dusko Tadic came into that room, sat down in the room and started to beat prisoners. One would have thought that all those other witnesses relating to paragraph 6 or who have come before this Court who were in the electrical workshop would have remembered that, would have given the Court evidence about that, if it happened. Significantly on that day, Dusko Tadic was on duty at the Orlovci checkpoint between 3.00 and 9 o'clock in the evening, so from a 3 p.m. shift to a 9 p.m. shift during the day. But there we have it. Here we have a witness who enters the Court, gives this evidence, no doubt many would have felt, "Well, that seems right, that has a flavour about it. After all he has come here to make his complaint, and to give his evidence and he can leave the Court room with that aura and respect for a victim that one has". But it is not until you piece together the whole of the case that you see the flaws in this kind of evidence, and one is entitled to look at it with criticism and caution when one bears in mind the actual context in which the allegation takes place. The electrical workshop by the hangar, Dusko Tadic going into the room, sitting down, beating prisoners, not concealing himself, being there, being seen, and we have other witnesses from that place who gave evidence before this Court. Edin Mrkalj who gave evidence of a beating on 16th June ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, your Honour, I have several references for redactions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We just handled two, I suppose, but four different places?

utterances.speaker: MISS FEATHERSTONE
utterances.text: Perhaps can you do them for the record?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Give us the cite to them.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: For the record, your Honour, they will be 10.07.52, that is one time, 10.09.08 as another and 10.09.20.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Kay. Mr. Mrkalj?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A 16th June beating within the administration building of Omarska. A witness whom Dusko Tadic knew as a police officer, but for some reason asked him what his job was when he came across him within the administration building before, apparently, assaulting him. He conceded that Tadic looked different on that day. It was something he had mentioned in a statement, that his appearance had changed. Again, is this a case (and it is for the Court to consider) of appearance of people who might look familiar or seem familiar but are not the same person within the context of how these four people were kept prisoners, in fact, suggestion replacing fact and truth, suggestion having a great power?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, are you going to give us the names of the other prisoners who were in the electrical workshop on 20th June and did not speak of Tadic being there and beating prisoners, because otherwise we will have to go through the entire transcript and try to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can do that at an appropriate time elsewhere within the notes ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- which I have now turned over! At this stage I would like to make a point about the so-called karate kick which the Prosecution have used as an identifying feature. It seems to us that virtually every male within opstina Prijedor undertook karate lessons. They all seemed to have been on the courses and they all seem to know about it. It may well be a feature of this society that that is something that the young men undertake. But it is by no means a rare occurrence for someone to have undertaken such lessons. One considers other districts of the world and you think how many people have had karate lessons within particular areas, it seems to be very much a common feature of their society and what young men undertook, perhaps even as part of their JNA training. In those circumstances, to give it a degree of importance or identifying feature, it is by no means an exclusive hallmark that could be applied. If Dusko Tadic was the only karate exponent within the district, it would have far greater significance than it, in fact, does.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, can you help me with that? I do not recall that line of testimony, that is, that taking karate was something that young men typically did and perhaps even as a part of their JNA training. If you can give me the names of some witnesses or some clue as to how I can find it in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Elvir Grozdanic went to karate classes, the karate classes in Kozarac, many of whom as young men in their teens had passed through the classes in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I recall that some witnesses testified that they had taken lessons from Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But other than that, I do not remember. If you can give us the citings, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. The mothers of some young men who said they took their sons there for karate training. It is something that we have noticed has been a thread throughout the case. Hasiba Harambasic is another Omarska sighting that deserves comment. This is a witness who said that she saw Dusko Tadic in mid July and certainly he was on duty at Orlovci during that time, so there is no way that we can tie down to see if there is a contradiction between the sighting and where on the face of it he was on duty. Significantly, an application has been made by the Prosecution in the form of a motion concerning an apparent inconsistency by this witness in relation to her testimony of not knowing Dusko Tadic but saying to a journalist that she did know -- that she did not know him. So there we have it: Brief sightings, sightings in difficult circumstances, a whole range of them, some with apparent flaws, and yet it is easy to say until one looks at the whole panoply of the case. There is also Trnopolje, a number of single sightings; one witness venturing some 20 plus sightings from the period of September 29th to late November 1992. She was a witness, Advija Campara, who was in the same building as the Jakupovics, Nasiha and Adil, who knew Dusko Tadic so well and whom he visited on one occasion at the camp in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, can I just interrupt you whilst you are dealing with Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: You referred us to the sightings in Omarska but, according to my reckoning, there were actually 25 sightings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: But you have only referred to some of them. What about the others?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I was taking economically if I could, your Honour, because I made the general point about circumstances which I did not want to repeat on each particular witness. I was putting the point before the Court and, in those circumstances, having made the submission, hoping that the Court would apply those observations that we have to the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I could certainly go through each of them, and the material has been prepared, but in a way it becomes repetitive because of the circumstances and the briefness. I have highlighted there a few with particular difficulties, that have problems, we say, within the genuineness of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you saying, Mr. Kay, that these witnesses lied, that they did not see Mr. Tadic or are you saying that they do not remember what he wore, because I am trying to remember what I wore yesterday. I do -- I remember part of it. It is difficult, is it not? So how should we look at this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is difficult, your Honour, and in a way it is a combination of things that we would say, there is mistake, error, genuine error. I would say some are made up. I would say in relation to particularly one of the witnesses who came here who had claimed a number of sightings and then withdrew them, the Prosecution said to him, to their own witness, "You have made allegations of seeing Dusko Tadic on more than one occasion and you now withdraw those?" That was a witness at Keraterm, Sefik Kesic, and he stuck by one identification. He said that he was less than sure about the others. He stuck by one identification alleging a beating that took place at night, with the lights of a vehicle down at the gate by Keraterm shining behind the man, beating him and, in those circumstances, stuck by an identification. Perhaps claims that have been made, there has been a need to stick by them having said something, having claimed to be part of what happened and to have seen the defendant. Perhaps there is a need to justify what one has said to a certain degree, but not to the extent that is a great deal. When I get to the evidence of Mehmed Alic, I will make that particular point, we hope, forcefully. So, it is a combination of things, your Honour, and we believe, for instance, in that example I gave of Mehmedalija Huskic that that is a classic example that the Court should be wary about.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Which one was that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is the electrical workshop on 20th June, a couple of days ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. So it is a combination of matters that we say. It is easy for these allegations to be made. Trnopolje itself is now a difficult subject before the Court, because there is no evidence of Dusko Tadic being in control of that camp or being responsible for its running, as seemed to have been a feature of the Prosecution case until the matters concerning Witness L were exposed. There is a witness who claims 20 plus sightings within that same building that the Jakupovics are, who know him well but only claim to have seen him once. Why she so specially would have seen him so many more times than anyone else, we say, is open to suspicion. A number of dotted around sightings of Trnopolje, some of which the Defence, as the Court knows, concedes, some five visits to the camp or just outside the camp during the period between June to October or November 1992. But, in the context of this case now, it is something that we suggest has no great deal of significance in view of the issues that the Court is trying and the allegations within the indictment. Even if those sightings are right, where at the end of the day does it leave the Court in terms of the indictment and allegations at Trnopolje against this defendant, killings and rapes that we were originally concerned with having gone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, does that mean that no other witnesses talk of particular acts of violence by the accused at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is right. That is right, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But I suppose it would be said by the Prosecution to the extent that he was at Trnopolje and there were acts of violence committed by others, that he was in some way a participant?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is insufficient, we say, because someone else commits something on another day and no nexus has been made to this defendant, we say, falls woefully short of evidence that the Court should accept as active participation, participation in any form, of any events that took part in Trnopolje. Originally, we were concerned with those killings and rapes and that is why it was such an important part, but there is no other evidence of rapes that remain with this case and no other evidence of killings at Trnopolje that remain in this case. But we have these sporadic sightings alleged by witnesses. To be frank about it, we say, well, where does that really take the Court in relation to the allegations?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, does it go to veracity, credibility? Witness -- I do not remember his name; I can see him in my mind; he became the Secretary of SDS after Mr. Tadic, I believe, in Kozarac, Secretary of the Local Commune ---

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- he had come from Velika Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Dusan ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He was a tall, thin, nice looking man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- yes, Dusan Vajgic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He testified, I thought -- of course, I do not remember his name but I do remember the testimony -- that the commune in Kozarac had no responsibility for Trnopolje, that Trnopolje was a separate commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Witness Y, also from Velika Kladusa and then of course moving to Kozarac, said that Mr. Tadic had not gone to Trnopolje, that they had no business, that is, those policemen in Kozarac had no responsibility over Trnopolje and no business being in Trnopolje. Another witness also I think said that. Of course, now Mr. Tadic has indicated in his alibi notice that he had gone to Trnopolje I think once, and then I do not recall the number of times that he told the German police that he had gone to Trnopolje. Then, of course, he testified, I think, five or six times going to Trnopolje. Then Mrs. Campara then testified she sees him approximately 20 times. Does it go to veracity, credibility, perhaps to all of those witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, in his alibi notice Dusko Tadic has two occasions. There is an issue here of where the camp begins and ends which is something we had as a problem within the evidence. In evidence he gave five occasions when he was at what would be broadly called the camp, be it in the lane outside or by the gate. To the German police five times was the occasion that he gave. The evidence of the witness Campara, we say, is so much extraordinarily out on a limb in terms of the numbers when you would have expected others to have seen him just as much as her. For that reason, I particularly cite the Jakupovic's who knew him and were there longer than she; that her every other day I think she was eventually increasing it to, which would put the figure at some 30 plus sightings, we say, is just something being said by a witness perhaps not with the best of motives or intentions in relation to this defendant. But the role of Dusko Tadic at this time in relation to the Local Commune in Kozarac which was supported by those witnesses, I suppose they only go so far as their own knowledge. They were not with him all the time, so when they say he did not visit Trnopolje that is as far as they can say. They cannot say any more than that. But they had great dealings with him during this period of time and were aware of his responsibilities and his jobs, and where those would have taken him. But certainly, as far as the defendant is concerned, he concedes going to Trnopolje. The interesting feature is that when he goes with the old man, Jovo Samardzija, he does not appear to go there with any kind of authority or any kind of status to help that man find his sister. He is just down there. He is not able to order people to go looking for Samardija's sister or cause doors to open or wheels to turn. He is just down there and waiting. They are talking to people whom they obviously knew within the camp. In our submission, that is an important feature of the Defence case that the Court will have to weigh in opposition to the allegations concerning Trnopolje. Moving still through 4.3 of the indictment, I have referred to the beatings in Keraterm between 25th May and 8th August of which two witnesses gave testimony, Sefik Kesic and Hakija Elezovic. This was the witness I have already referred to your Honour Judge Vohrah about as being an example that a witness gives an account and then withdraws a number of allegations, but is sticking by one in circumstances ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I thought you were still on 4.2. You have been on 4.3 for some time, have you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: They seem to ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am still on 4.2. Thank you. I must say actually -- I only say this in my own defence -- there are a number of repetitions within these paragraphs of the indictment that can easily cause a mistake. Yes, looking at 4.2 still, and I have made the point about the beatings within Keraterm being only two occasions and there are circumstances to doubt the accuracy of the Sefik Kesic allegation. Hakija Elezovic is that important witness who gives evidence in relation to count 8, charge 8, paragraph 8, of the indictment, who claims to have been present when his son was killed. It does seem peculiar that at his interview in Keraterm he names Dusko Tadic for some reason being present as a bodyguard. Quite why and for what reason one does not know, unless it is perhaps to pin this defendant. It may come down to that, putting it bluntly, and your Honour, Judge McDonald, has asked me about the motives or reasons why stories should be given. Quite why he should be there if he is doing these other things in the area as an attendant to the interrogator at this man's interview, one wonders. It does not seem to be that he was particularly important in any form or to any degree, if the profile as presented by the Prosecution of Dusko Tadic is right, to waste his time sitting in on the interview of this man. But there we have it. It was an allegation made, an allegation easily sold, perhaps, but one has to wonder about buying it. Moving through ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: What date was that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: 27th?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 27th July. I think it is just before because he went to Keraterm first and then Omarska.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sorry, I thought you were talking about Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is mid July, I think about 20th July, as I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Still on 4.2, we make this point within the text of the indictment, that there is no evidence of looting of belongings of detainees in Keraterm between 25th May and 8th August 1992. I have pointed out to the Court the four witnesses who give evidence concerning Dusko Tadic's presence at Keraterm. There is no evidence of looting, extorting, taking belongings from those detainees. The Court will have to consider whether the single occasion outlined by Sefik Kesic when he was part of a group of 10 men lined up, for the purposes of this case and this kind of trial, would also come within a category of mass beatings of detainees in room 2 between that same period. Kesic claims to have been part of 10 prisoners at night time with the lights of the car behind them who were part of a group for some reason individually beaten by Dusko Tadic, one after another, for no apparent purpose or reason. Nothing was sought to be obtained. They were just taken from the room, apparently, if this witness is to be believed, and this man alone committed these acts, the only man named. We say the reason why he is the only man named is he was the only man, perhaps, at a certain time against whom allegations were being made and who was in captivity. But the Court will have to consider whether that qualifies for a war crimes trial as evidence of mass beating. I have now concluded 4.2, and move to 4.3 of the indictment and will be able to proceed more rapidly through these allegations, because in part they have been dealt with by my submissions on 4.1. But the transfer to Trnopolje camp of non-Serbs in the Kozarac area between the dates of 25th May and 31st December, this is largely the evidence of Nasiha Klipic and Mehmed Alic, Zikina's and Limenka's on 26th and 27th May. Again we say there is no evidence of Dusko Tadic being responsible for the unlawful confinement of prisoners within the camp. That would have held together if Witness L's allegations had been pursued with, and perhaps it is a feature that I must stress here because other than he who described him at one stage as having authority within the camp, that does not seem to be anything that has come through from the material of the witnesses that we have heard. I have to say a few words about Witness L here because when your Honour, Judge McDonald, asked me about the reason for making allegations, perhaps we have it in a microcosm in relation to this witness who came into the Court, made these allegations. At that stage, perhaps, people left the courtroom believing him. Certainly the Prosecution would have believed him, otherwise they would not have called him. I am not going to ask anyone to put their hands up to confess whether they believed him and found him a credible or acceptable witness, but one must bear in mind that the power of giving evidence in a Court such as this and speaking, perhaps, about horrific acts, carries with it a specially resonant message and often the more graphic -- we are all human beings -- we are often sympathetic and receptive to such material and find ourselves in a position more easily to believe, but we know because we went through this process with great difficulty that he was exposed as a liar. But that was possible in a way because that was within our province, within our territory. We could investigate in the area of Kozarac. We could get a form of co-operation. A lot of it came out of chance and luck, but that was something that we were able to get into and step by step and piece by piece put this material before the Court. At the end of it, in our submission, the Prosecution very honourably and quite rightly took a pragmatic course in relation to those allegations. But above all this case we say there should be almost a sticker put up: "Don't forget Witness L, don't forget what happened there". It serves as a reminder to us all and a graphic illustration of what can happen and how easy it can be to make allegations such as that and they, unfortunately, not be the truth. I will move now to 4.4 of the indictment. As I have said, there is a great deal of repetition within count 1. We have an example of that here with the participation in the seizure and selection of individuals for detention in the camps and transportation of Muslims and Croats who had been seized to the camps for detention. During the time he was engaged in this seizure, selection and transfer of non-Serbs, Dusko Tadic was aware that they would be deported. The principal witnesses here are Nasiha Klipic, Mehmed Alic, whom I have dealt with in relation to the 26th and 27th May, and then we have the Sivci and Jaskici collection of witnesses for 14th June 1992 that make up paragraph 12 of the indictment. For that purpose, I will deal with this evidence now so that the Court can have perhaps the Omarska allegations dealt with as a whole and will conclude my submissions before the Bench. Paragraph 12 of the indictment that fits into this section of the count 1 persecution count is 14th June, and starts in Sivci as the population, the male population, is rounded up. We had a video showing us the extent of the village of Sivci, a long drawn out village with the Mekteb, with the various farms, houses and the courtyard where a lot of the men were collected, and nearby on the other side of the road what is a stream or a brook flowing down the road and where there were buses that the men were put on. The one witness in relation to this matter was a man called Sakib Sivac and he gave evidence that the population was rounded up between 1 o'clock in the afternoon and 3 o'clock in the afternoon. It must have been quite an operation as there were quite a few hundred males involved. The Court will remember evidence of the men moving down the street, being made to go down on the ground, get up, run, go down on the ground, get up, run -- obviously done as some kind of control, command, over these people to exert a form of discipline. Then the men were put in the buses that had arrived. This particular witness was on the last bus, and he got in through the rear doors and there claimed to have seen Dusko Tadic and Dragolje Cavic. He said he looked into the eyes of the man he knew as Dusko Tadic and claimed to have recognised him wearing a new camouflage uniform without a cap, a rifle with a folding butt which was something that he noticed, handcuffs on the belt and a beard of 15 days to one month's growth. The conclusion of this would have been around 3 o'clock, as he told the Court. He did not have access to any sort of time piece, and that is his best estimate of the time. Again we put this before the Court. If this man Dusko Tadic was the man who was single-handedly running the cleansing of Kozarac, if he was in positions of control and authority, that the profile the Prosecution have presented to us is right, it seems a bit peculiar that he is performing some menial, unimportant role in relation to this operation, guarding the back doors of the bus and not giving the orders, not telling people what to do. It does not fit into that profile they have presented. But again this is one of those circumstances of a recognition that is very hard for the Defence to get underneath. But we also have side by side with these allegations this 3 o'clock at Jaskici, the rounding up of the male population within that hamlet nearby. We say there seems to be an overlap of time here. 3 o'clock is, apparently, a reliable time as one of the witnesses, Sena Jaskic, said she recollected the news coming on the radio and that is how she was able to pin point it. From the events that took place, that seems to have been the first house that was entered by the soldiers and where it was alleged a man was taken out and moved up the lane. Is Dusko Tadic in Sivci or Jaskici? Bear in mind this. Those women who gave evidence described him being with a group of soldiers, many of whom they described as being in black, dressed up in black clothes. That may be a form of dress that is particularly easy to remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But there is no definite time at which Sakib Sivac says that he was in the first of the two villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: So why do you say that there is a surprising overlap?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I do not think I used the word "surprising". There is an overlap. I may have used the word "surprising".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It surprised me that you said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. There could well be here, is this yet another case of multiple sightings of Dusko Tadic at the same time as we showed in Kozarac for the morning of 26th May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Because they are only 10 minutes apart walking, are they not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. When I throw in the other descriptions of that day, this is why we say it comes clear, not both these places can be right. Who knew him the better? On the Prosecution case, Sakib Sivac or the ladies confronted with this extremely distressing piece of history, because they describe the soldiers being in black with Dusko Tadic, and that was not a feature of the Sivci allegations. So, looking at the whole of this, somewhere another unit has come along of which he is suddenly now in control, having previously been what amounts to an unimportant role as guarding the back of the bus, quite why are there these two different roles? They do not support that profile that we have put before the Court as described by the Prosecution. We have identification problems here of these witnesses from Jaskici of, we would say, a serious nature. Draguna Jaskic, who is the first recognition witness that gave evidence, and the photospread and saying she did not recognise anyone at the time. But we have the report of the investigator who only undertook one of these particular procedures saying that her eyes dilated, there was a sharp intake of breath, and much later her saying that she had, in fact, identified Dusko Tadic within that bundle of photos although, on the face of it, at the time said, no. That would certainly fail one of Professor Wagenaar's tests and, as he said, would not be a valid identification. Subha Mujcic is another witness who was the second to give the recognition evidence, again describing soldiers in black, two wearing masks, and giving the broadly same description of a green camouflage uniform. But of all these witnesses the one who had the longest period for identification was the witness Zemka Sahbaz who Miss Hollis described yesterday identifying while she was at the house, and then also looking up the lane to see what was happening and then eventually under fear going back into her house. She describes a blond boy with a stick beating the men taken prisoner. The previous witness had described Dusko Tadic, Draguna Jaskic had described Dusko Tadic, as having a stick or a pole and beating the men. Again if Sakib Sivac is right, that did not appear to be something that he had with him when he was seen in Sivci during the loading on of the men from Sivci on to the buses. So where did this come from? How did that suddenly appear with him? That witness, Zemka Sahbaz, gives a description of a uniform that varied in colour. The Court will remember the evidence about this varying from blue, coffee and green, but the great point (and a point that she was trying to evade under cross-examination because she knew that she had said it before) was that the hat as being worn by Dusko Tadic had a wide brim. So where did he acquire that? He did not have a hat on in Sivci. But this witness who saw him the longest, apparently, said that he was wearing a hat with a wide brim. Something such as that, a distinguishing feature, throws, we say, this evidence into turmoil and causes us again to question whether the unfortunate events that happened to these people require a victim of a different sort now and that is the man on trial. The photospread that was put before her, Zemka Sahbaz, who did not know Dusko Tadic, again has a serious flaw. It was 31st May 1996, almost four years later and after this trial had started, but she describes the man with the stick or pole as being a man with blond hair, and she described the man moving the soldiers up the lane. The Prosecution have helpfully pieced together those events of the afternoon with that helpful board with the houses on and the progress up the road and where everyone lived. It was one man who was in charge of these soldiers moving the men up the road, the one said to be Dusko Tadic, and this witness said wearing a wide hat, a hat with a wide brim. Further up the lane, we have a sighting by Senija Elkasovic as she looked out of the window in what were fairly perilous and risky circumstances, and she said seeing Dusko Tadic in her courtyard and then moving across the yard. Again there were colour changes in the uniforms. So there we have it with those events on that particular day. We ask this Court to have great caution about the evidence because of this variance of the testimonies of the witnesses, and not everyone can be right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I will ask this question of the Prosecution and I suppose it is just my thinking constantly about different concerns, including the cause of the conflict, now we are talking about identification. For the Prosecution witnesses and the Defence witnesses, I do not recall a witness ever saying, "I do not recall what he was wearing", and that really surprised me. As I went through I heard -- I do not know whether it was cultural thing -- witnesses from the Prosecution, I heard witnesses from the Defence, describing in their mind with exactitude what people were wearing. I found that rather amazing, based on my prior experience. I just have not seen it. Maybe you can help me. You have been to the former Yugoslavia. Is this something that people there attempt to make an estimate of what people were wearing, where they were and whether they had a hat on? Maybe I am just used to hearing people say over and over, "I do not recall, I do not recall".

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So maybe we have moved ahead in this Tribunal, but everyone has an opinion. Help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The majority of witnesses did, in fact, give descriptions of clothing.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: On both sides?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Some witnesses, in fact, did say they could not remember and there were those and did not attempt to give dates. But ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, I was really talking more about description.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I am seeking here not to make distinctions between olive green, coffee, pale and whatever. Of course, we lay those before the Court for the Court's consideration, but I am seeking here to point out single distinguishing features that, perhaps, transcend clothing, that are part of the sight and the picture of the man going up the lane. This is where we would say an article of distinctive clothing that is not a description of clothes, but what was being worn to that degree is so far out of the norm and at variance with what one would generally allow for margins of error that the Court should bear that in mind as, perhaps, not being a matter that could be more easily moved over when one confuses browns and olives and greens, which one can understand mistakes like that being made. But you get such significant descriptions of items of clothing that are outside that broad brush of error, margins of error, that one would permit. For that purpose, we certainly draw those matters to the Court's attention. Things like a headband or not a headband is quite significant. Seeing a man with a headband is something one, perhaps, remarks and notices. You do not see everyone wearing headbands. I suppose it depends what district you live in, but most people do not see in their areas many headbands and it is a cause for observation.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: These witnesses were, I think, all related or certainly a goodly number of them were, all sisters, sisters-in-law, widows, so when I heard them -- I will just tell you what goes through my mind when I heard them coming in, I said, "Well, they are all related. Let me listen very carefully to this" because that is one of the things when I was talking to Mr. Wladimiroff about cross-examination and what you show by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then, though, when I hear the different descriptions, I say, "Well, my goodness, if they wanted to get together, why did they not do a better job of all just reciting in rote what he looked like?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, if they all sat down at a meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: They all had the opportunity if they wanted to make it up. I was listening to their testimony with caution and understanding that they were all related, because I feel it is something that I should do. But now I hear, you know, if they really wanted to make it up, they would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: They may have been sent to the far corners of the globe and be in different countries for all we know, and may be one or two have spoken in terms of consistency. I asked Draguna Jaskic over her non-identification or identification, as the Prosecution would say, whether she had spoken to anyone else. There is that tendency. One remark may influence another. But it is impossible for us, given our access to these people and the circumstances of the case, which is why -- I hope I am not boring the Court with repeating this caution part of my submission, because we are not in control of where they are. In an ordinary jurisdiction -- let me just take London -- you understand the area, you are able to go around the are, you are able to perhaps piece together your defence and investigate rather more satisfactorily. Because of the events that have happened here, that is not possible. These people, as we know, are flung around the globe. They are no longer still at the site from which the allegations arise. So, the usual processes that are possible for Prosecution and Defence to consider matters such as that, your Honour, are not available. That is why this trial is a very unusual trial, and we say great caution has to be applied by your Lordships in looking at this evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are not boring me and maybe I am just asking you to do my job for me, but I am just telling you what my thought processes were. Of course, when you hear persons testify who are related, then you have to keep in mind possible bias. Then when I hear the discrepancies, I do not know whether that helps or hurts, but I understand your position that there are discrepancies in terms of their description of what Mr. Tadic was wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. One misidentification, of course, can cause a chain reaction if reported and relied upon by others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, can I ask you this, and you may not know the answer, but the curious uniform, black t-shirts, black trousers and sinister gloves with the fingers protruding, does any of that match any description that we have had of particular paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: None are called to mind, but I think within (and going back a long way now) the policy section of the Prosecution case there may well have been a reference to groups who wear ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Who wore black.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- that kind of uniform. Others may be better able to advise the Court about that, but it may well be they were connected with many of the Arkan groups or other names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That is what I was wondering, whether you had any knowledge of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Did the witness testify it was in Prijedor? Did he testify about people coming in dressed like that? Do you recall? We will check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: We also had, did we not, some misunderstanding months ago about wearing a mask ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: --- and that was simply a misunderstanding in translation for camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: The mask that one witness speaks of the people in Jaskici wearing, that is not a misunderstanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is a mask mask and not the camouflage mask. Certainly we accept that there is this misunderstanding capable within the language because of the phrases used. It is something that we would not seek to put before the Court as being of importance. Moving now to paragraph 4.5 of the indictment, which is a series of allegations, first of all, expressing allegations about the Serb forces, but most particularly concerning the period between 23rd May and 31st August 1992 Dusko Tadic was aware of the widespread nature of the plunder and destruction of personal and real property for non-Serbs and was physically involved and participated in that plunder and destruction, including the plunder of homes in Kozarac and the looting of valuables from non-Serbs as they were seized and upon their arrival at the camps and detention centres. This section of the indictment, we submit, needs particular care in looking at by the Court. There is evidence by the witness Minerva Kulasic, a rebuttal witness, page 6327, of the plunder of personal property. This concerns the home that had been previously occupied by the Chief of Police and her mother, sister and she are ejected from it. There is evidence there before the Court of the plunder of that property, if that witness is right. The Defence case was slightly different, admitting the taking of the property but saying that the goods were returned. But there is no evidence of the physical involvement of Dusko Tadic in the destruction of property of non-Serbs. There has been no evidence about that at all before the Court. There has also been no evidence of the physical involvement in the plunder and destruction of houses in Kozarac by Dusko Tadic. The nearest one could get to it, I suppose, would be the firing of the flares on 24th May to enable the shelling of the hospital. But the indictment specifically says "physical involvement by him", so the allegation that we say is being made to the Court is that he was destroying homes by blowing them up or plundering them. I had to remind myself what the word "plunder" meant not being a word that one comes across regularly in terms of criminal law these days -- I suppose many centuries ago you did -- and its definition is robbery, to rob. There was also no evidence before the Court in relation to this section of the indictment of the physical involvement of Dusko Tadic in looting valuables from non-Serbs that were seized upon arrival at Omarska, Keraterm and Trnopolje. There has simply been no evidence about that. We take issue with one of the legal concepts within this section of the indictment concerning real property which, we say, cannot be plundered. You cannot steal land. You can steal cars, you can steal rings, wallets. You cannot take the land away with you. There are other offences which take into account obtaining real property by deception or other means, but within the jurisdictions that we are familiar with, this concept of plundering land, robbing a plot of land, is not something that we say is possible and the Court should consider that as a legal issue.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Just two questions. Was the hospital actually shelled? I think a shell fell but nearby. Did it hit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think there was later evidence that said it was hit. Quite whether it was as a result of the flares, I do not know, because the witness himself would not have been going back to the hospital then as he was on his way down -- or did he return? I am slightly lost there, your Honour, but, yes, your Honour is right to make that observation.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: My second question is regarding the plundering of real property: would that not include the taking of homes that belong to Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is a concept of stealing land, whether you can do that in ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I mean a home, a real property, a home affixed to the land?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, that is real property.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Plundering would not include, then, the taking of homes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Is that so? Do you not constantly, well, in reading histories, hear of the plundering of a city, and that means going into the city and taking things from homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Looting, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, plundering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Robbing, but the taking of the town hall ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: No, no, but going into the town hall and taking the mirrors and the furniture ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Possible

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: --- is plundering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But you cannot plunder real property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is what you are doing. You are going into the town hall and plundering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, real property being realty, being land.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: All the fixtures on the land.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is personalty, that is goods person ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: The building is personalty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The building is realty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, and you go into the realty and plunder it by taking things from it -- no?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But you take out the personalty and personalty is ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I think this is -- yes, well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I must say I left my chancery law days some time ago. I hope that is not being repeated on air! But, your Honour, I have finished this particular section now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes. 11.30 a.m.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Now I move to paragraph 6 of the indictment and commence submissions on the remaining substantive counts that deal with crimes within Omarska. Just while I am here a matter your Honour Judge Stephen raised concerning other witnesses who had been downstairs in the electrical workshop at this period of time who would be able to provide evidence concerning other matters that could have occurred in that room concerning Dusko Tadic, Armin Kenjar, Muharem Besic, Elvir Grozdanic, Emsud Velic, and Ferid Mujcic, all of whom are within the paragraph 6 allegations concerning Omarska. Many witnesses have claimed to know what happened on that afternoon which more probably than not was 18th June 1992. Some 14 witnesses claimed to have seen and/or heard some part of the events that occurred on that fateful day. All of them relate in graphic detail the horror that was experienced at the time in the heart of what really was that spiritual darkness within that hangar of the building in Omarska. One of the problems as we see it facing this Court is that this allegation has achieved such notoriety, has been talked about so widely, perhaps relived so many times, that perhaps the truth has become obscured and so that mistakes or false statements that have been made are given the status of truth that many witnesses have been willing to lend their names to in support. When witness G returned from the hangar -- and many witnesses have told the Court about the mental instability of that young man -- and he returned to the prisoners' area covered in oil and in a highly emotional state, perhaps he hit a spark that fired a rumour that swept through the rooms elsewhere within the hangar. The rumour was that it was Dusko Tadic that afternoon who was the man who caused him to commit an act of unimaginable savagery on a fellow prisoner, and that was the biting off of the testicle of a living man and he may well have claimed far more besides. The rumour in that camp almost spread like a forest fire and all who heard them were, no doubt, convinced of the truth of the rumour. But there was another participant in that horrific scene who returned to the prisoners' rooms after G. That witness had been in the hangar longer. He had been there for more than an hour and he returned to tell the truth, as he knew it to be, and perhaps by then was a small, still voice in a situation that was not calm, and the truth about the man with the beard who was giving orders was that it was not Dusko Tadic but a man he did not know. By then no calming influence, perhaps, would have been possible because of the horror that had happened. Already when he returned, people were asking him if it was Dule, if it was Dusko Tadic, in other words. As he told this Court, he told them that he was not there. He did not see Dusko Tadic. He was an eyewitness and a participant. So we must consider the reliability and whether his observation of events is any better than any of the other witnesses. We are setting eyewitness against others who were in the area at the time. This witness H had been ordered around the hangar. He had been ordered to drag bodies up and down the hangar. He had been ordered to lie down, stand up and do push ups. He had been ordered to jump into the canal and drink oil. He had been ordered to hold the head of Fikret Harambasic whilst he had been sexually mutilated by G. He had seen a young guard in a uniform when he had asked for two volunteers and he had recognised that young guard. He had seen a bearded man who selected him as a volunteer, and witness G -- well, not witness G, as G as a volunteer. He had seen that that man wore a green military uniform. He had seen puddles of blood. He had seen the body of Emir Karabasic. He had seen the body of Jasmin Hrnic. He had seen the body of Eno Alic. He had seen where their bodies lay. He had seen the soldiers had gathered around the garage door. He had seen a guard called Bakar (who is important for another reason that I will address the Court upon when I look at what the witnesses say), this man with a scar on his face and whom he and others knew. He had seen the faces of the guards. He knew the guards were from Krkan's shift, what has become known as the notorious shift of guards. He had seen Fikret Harambasic naked and with a battered body climb into the canal where he and witness G were and he had seen witness G bite off Fikret Harambasic's testicle during a fairly considerable period of time. He had seen him spit that part of his body out and that it went down a drain. He had seen where it went. He had seen the guard who set him free. No matter how the Prosecution have attempted to present before this Court a witness blinkered, moving around the hangar unseeing, unknowing, all that background of his participation and how he was involved speaks against the presentation of his evidence in that way, because, as he said, he did not see Dusko Tadic. So we must look at what really happened on that afternoon and consider how reliable witnesses are. The only man to have his testicle bitten off by G was Fikret Harambasic. That is an important feature relating to the evidence on this matter. H, as the eyewitness, was able to tell the Court about that because he and G moved out into that hangar together. We say the litmus test of witnesses' evidence on this matter to determine whether they saw or heard any part of this sexual torture is whether they knew Fikret Harambasic was the victim. That is an important feature of the events that happened, was that for that to happen he was naked, and that is the evidence about him getting into the canal. For this sexual mutilation to take place, he had to be unclothed. He had to be naked to enable it to occur as it did. There is no evidence of those other victims, Karabasic, Alic or Hrnic also being naked. Witnesses who identify the acts of G as being performed on any of those three men are not victims or witnesses who really knew what happened. That is why we say it is a litmus test in relation to the reliability of these accounts, because this Court is faced with the participant eyewitness standing in contradiction to the other witnesses who claim to have seen or heard either some of the events earlier, more adjacent to the time, or just after it. Witness H was familiar with Dusko Tadic with a beard and without a beard. He had known him and was able to say he was able to distinguish, he knew him in both forms of appearance. He starts events in that position down at the stairwell when he is near the door and he saw the guard who called out Jasko Hrnic. Again, a particular feature of this evidence that we say is an important indicator for the Court is that the name "Asko" was used not "Jasko". The evidence has been of the friendship in the past between Hrnic and Tadic. "Asko" would not have been a mistake that Tadic would have made. "Asko" would not have been required to have been called by Tadic, but "Jasko". Even if someone makes a mistake once, if Tadic was there he would have corrected that to the man calling out the names. "Jasko" is the name, the name that he knew so well. Again, this is something that within the whole context of this matter we attribute great importance to. Witness H also saw Alic go past him, Meho Alic, and then return with his son Enver. So there was no participation of detainees in sexual mutilation until after those three had gone out there into the hangar. It was Fikret Harambasic who was the victim of that. Importantly, he heard a prisoner being ordered to eat a pigeon before he went out there. That is whilst he was still down there in what I will call the stairwell, that section behind the doors where the stairs take you to the upper rooms. That was not an event that occurred whilst he was out there in the hangar with G. Fikret Harambasic was not required to eat a pigeon, neither was G, neither was H. That was an occasion before he went out, but what he saw whilst he was down there. We must take it that he would have been more likely to have been at the forefront of any people in the stairwell, because the volunteers, one would imagine, are the more immediate people, and "volunteers" is an expression that has been used but we know they were not really. So, he by those doors would have had a good view of what was happening, calling out Jasko Hrnic, the eating of the pigeon, the people out there in the hangar before he entered that particular arena to play his unfortunate and fateful part. He knew he did not see Dusko Tadic during that period before he had gone out into the hangar. He was taken out after Karabasic, Hrnic and Alic had been beaten. Their bodies were laying virtually lifeless on the ground by that stage. Certainly he believed only one had the remnants of life remaining. We have this ghastly scene of him dragging the bodies of Hrnic and Alic around the hangar. Those were not the bodies of men with any life left in them by that stage. That had passed. They were not the bodies of men able to stand or walk. They were just lying on the ground and he indicated to the Court whereabouts in relation to the canals. He knew where those bodies lay. So, in the view of his evidence as an eyewitness, giving, we would say, powerful testimony on this matter, we must now look at the evidence of others who claim to have seen or heard or been around when these events took place. Perhaps we will start with Halid Mujkanovic, another from the stairwell where he was selected. He did not identify Fikret Harambasic, but he said it could have been a man who was Emir Karabasic that he saw in a canal. He is obviously not clear about the identity of any person he saw whilst he remained peeping through his fingers and hiding himself, as he told us, at the bottom of the stairwell. We say, well, who would have had a better view of these events, Halid Mujkanovic or witness H, one hiding himself, peeping through fingers, the other a direct participant? It was his claim that a pigeon was given to the man being mutilated by G, so the pigeon after H says that happened. He said that Jasko Hrnic was standing and being beaten, but when G and H left the room we know that that was either a lifeless body or a virtually lifeless body that had to be dragged in that barbaric way up and down the hangar. He claims that in that position where he was, which must have been a considerable distance away and in those circumstances of fear, that he was able to see the incident that happened right the other side of the hangar. Interestingly enough, Bakar whom H identified as being present, the man with the scar on his face whom H recognised, he did not identify as being there. This particular guard, Bakar, had demanded money and beaten Mujkanovic, and he knew his name and was familiar with him; and yet for his apparent observation of this incident this guard whom he knew and to whom H gave some prominence because he was aware that he was there, he completely missed out. Of the people there whom one would have expected this witness to have seen, that would have been certainly one of them. Contrary to H, he did not recognise the guards as being those from the infamous Krkan shift. The only name he gave was of Dusko Tadic. We say that is because that name had spread like a wild fire. Armin Mujcic, the next witness I turn to, was sitting on a crate in the hangar and he goes into the stairwell from which G and H eventually emerge when the coloured ones arrive. That must have been sometime later. But he rushes from that area in great fear. I put this before the Court at this stage because we seem to have many people wandering around the hangar at this stage claiming to have seen various things, which is rather contrary to the evidence that they were only allowed to the lavatory at certain times. They had to ask permission and guards were exercising such control that these men were often frightened to leave their rooms. They were safer in the rooms rather than at the mercy of these men outside. But Armin Mujcic's description of the man he says was Dusko Tadic is a man wearing sunglasses and a cap, so what would, apparently, be a partially obscured face that he says was Dusko Tadic. Of all the various guises and forms of clothing, this is the only description in that form. He said it was a correct shift on duty rather than the Krkan shift who gave him this warning, and he just describes Dusko Tadic as arriving within the hangar and does not describe any of the beatings of the victims and omits, of course, from the three main victims of Karabasic, Hrnic and Alic, Beganovic and Muslimovic who were also part of this incident. He says that after the events had taken place, G and H returned up the stairs together whilst returning from the hangar, that they returned to the rooms in the first floor of these buildings within the hangar complex and that they came together, but we know from H, and he told us, he returned later after G. He was required to stay behind and he was near one of the bodies. He believed that Jasko Hrnic had been the victim of the sexual mutilation. Of course, we know it was Fikret Harambasic. He had spoken to G. He had seen the Monika Gras film which featured an interview with G and he did not speak to H. We say there is every indication here of a misidentification by that witness of Dusko Tadic. The next witness I turn to is Husein Hodzic. This is the witness upstairs in the room at the end of the corridor where a large number of prisoners were being held. He had said that Emir Karabasic at the time of the calling out had looked out of the window -- the photograph has been produced before the Court that there is one window that is not of opaque glass, but one window of clear glass -- and in looking out had said, "Dule has arrived, I'm finished." This Court is asked to, first of all, rely upon the reliability of that alleged sighting by the deceased Karabasic as providing a vital connection, and for some reason the specific name "Dule" is mentioned and yet there is no indication certainly that there had been any previous confrontation between Karabasic and Dusko Tadic within the camp. Why did he not, if he knew what was going to happen to him, say, "They have arrived"? Why should this particular victim have known that day that his name was going to be called out, or is this, unfortunately, a case where testimony is being given of almost famous last words, some final departing statement which has been lent to after the event? Because there are interesting reasons why we should say that about this particular testimony. He believed that Karabasic had been subject to, as he describes it, that monstrous act. By that we would reasonably imply the sexual mutilation which, of course, we know was Harambasic and not Karabasic. In his previous statement that he had given in July 1993, he had lent his name and authority to a far more detailed and graphic description of the incident. In that statement he claimed he had seen the whole incident, including Karabasic, Hrnic, Alic and Fikret Harambasic with witness G, but with no mention of H, the second man, perhaps by that stage the still, small and forgotten voice within those rooms upstairs in the hangar building. He claimed to have seen many details of what happened and when cross-examined about it said it was just a story that he had given, an account of events as he understood them to be. But the language of that statement, we submit, does not permit him that interpretation. The word "seen", "I saw", and description were not limited. They were being provided in direct form by him, not in indirect form. The one matter that he has called before this Court upon to provide the nexus between Tadic and Karabasic he did not mention in that statement, the last words of Emir Karabasic. He did not mention in that statement Dusko Tadic at all. He did not mention that he had been given this remark as that man walked out of the room to provide the connection, and there is no evidence of other witnesses within that room hearing the remark. So, he had on a previous occasion claimed to see things he had not, and did not mention these particular words which must have a great degree of significance. They are appealing as last remarks and last remarks can often be scripted. He has, perhaps, given a little something in the evidence in the case, but resiled from what he had claimed to have seen before. There is every motive after what these men had been through for them, unfortunately, to go down such a route. I now move to Elvir Grozdanic whose evidence, we say, is rather peculiar in its form, that he was wandering around the hangar as beatings were happening, perhaps in the Beganovic and Muslimovic phase of the assaults that afternoon. He was wandering around completely unseen and untouched, and when apparently previously Dusko Tadic who had had a confrontation with him over parking had, apparently, been looking for him and wanted to know if he was a particular policeman. He claims to have seen two dead bodies in the lavatories of the hangar building, and to pass by in close proximity to Dusko Tadic as he leaves those lavatories with a bloody stick. It was raised during Miss Hollis's submissions to the Court yesterday about the route, the apparent circuitous route, that Dusko Tadic would have had to have taken if he is right, moving down the hangar almost in a circle to get round to the electrical workshop, as he would have described it, as he moved from the lavatories down to that other end of the building. No matter how slowly, carefully, he was creeping around, one would have thought that he would have been presenting himself there as a target. As part of his evidence, because he must explain how he got back into the electrical workshop, he claims to have slipped through the door as Jasko Hrnic left, is quite clearly his evidence, and he goes to Jasko Hrnic's place in the room. None of those witnesses within that room have claimed anything of the sort that they saw a prisoner, even if they did not know his name, Elvir Grozdanic, that they saw a prisoner slipping through at the same time back into the room and go to the seat where Hrnic had been on that table in a recess that forms part of the room. Interestingly, he claims when he got there something had happened which had still not occurred by then. Armin Kenjar wrote the date 18/-6 an hour later, he had not written it then, but this witness claims that when he got there having slipped in through the door as Hrnic left, unseen by anybody, that he went to that section of the wall and saw there already written 18/-6. Well, that had not happened there and then, and we must take it that the man who admitted writing that on the wall and giving his reasons for doing it, which perhaps would have been after all the events had occurred, no one could say then that these men were going to be killed. We know Beganovic and Muslimovic survived. So he must be right about that, that he after it happened wrote that on the wall, but Grozdanic claimed that he saw it already there as he slipped through the door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
