utterances.text: Mr. Kay, the evidence is that part of what is now written from the photograph was written by Hrnic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Then the actual date put on subsequently?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: By Armin Kenjar at 7 o'clock and he wrote it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is the 18/-6 that this witness claimed to have seen when he sat in this place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: His statement given in Germany on a previous occasion was again of a totally different picture. He claimed that he saw Emir Karabasic, Fikret Harambasic, Eno Alic and Jasko Hrnic being called out. Quite why a translator should insert this into his statement we have difficulty understanding. It can only be information and representations given by him. When it was put to him that in that previous statement he said he saw the Monika Gras film, he denied that in court. When he said in his previous statement that he had spoken to G, he denied that in court. Was this witness claiming to see things that he did not, because as these events are taking place, which we know start earlier than Hrnic and Alic, with Beganovic and Muslimovic, would he really have been wandering around having food in a part of the hangar where quite a large number of these soldiers were gathering intent on committing torture? How was it possible? Or is he lending his name to something almost as a badge for Omarska? The Prosecution explanation relating to the evidence of this witness and his progress around the hangar, we submit with respect, defies belief. Muharem Besic is the next witness I turn to. He claimed that Dusko Tadic came to the door of the electrical workshop to call out Jasko Hrnic, and that Hrnic opened the door to let himself out. Again, the calling out of Hrnic is claimed by other witnesses, and most particularly, H, to have been in fact by a guard. The indicator of that is why Asko would have been sent first and not Jasko. But there we have it. He was at the back of the room, containing at that time in the electrical workshop 200 people. Even if that is an overestimate, for such a small space 100 people would be a lot, 50 people would be a lot. Again, as an indicator, we say, of this being a witness lending his name to events afterwards, he clearly thinks that the sexual mutilation took place on either Hrnic or Karabasic or Alic because of those words of "bite" and "suck" being spoken of as occurring at the time that they were outside. They were not those victims of sexual mutilation. They had probably just been beaten. He fails what we would say is the Fikret/Harambasic case. Sitting where he was right at the back of this room, why would he have any better view than someone present at the scene being H or any closer to the door? Emsud Velic was another one at the back of the electrical workshop and I turn to him now. He claimed that Tadic came into the door of the room and was looking all over the people for some 10 to 15 seconds. So we have witnesses in contradiction here, some saying a guard at the door with Tadic behind; others saying Tadic at the door, such as he, casting his eye over the people within; others saying the door only being opened to let out Hrnic and then the door closing, that those behind the door were concealing themselves; another witness who does not see Elvir Grozdanic coming into the room, and we would say he fails also the Asko test when that name was called out in that form. So, again, another different story that is before this Court. When he made his English statement in March 1996, and this was a witness the Court may well remember as being the witness who spoke in English. Right towards the end of the Prosecution case, I think the fifth or sixth last witness in August, he spoke in English and gave his evidence in English, and spoke very well. But he had made a statement in March 1996 claiming Jasmin and Alic were called from that room at the electrical workshop. His explanation was that he had been late in working and that there was tiredness, or has his evidence changed to fit an emerging picture that various people are seeking to put as a tableau of what happened on that day? He had spoken to G. In re-examination by Mr. Tieger he said that G had told him it was Jasko and Karaba with whom he had been involved. We know it was Fikret Harambasic. At the end of the day that witness in that position, is he reliable? Is there a consistency here, is there accuracy that the Court will need to be certain in relation to these allegations? Armin Kenjar is the next witness I turn to, and I have already spoken briefly about him writing on the wall. He claimed to have seen Dusko Tadic between the canals half an hour before Hrnic was called out. He contradicts Emsud Velic and others by putting a guard at the door and not Dusko Tadic when Hrnic is called out. Asko again is the test that we say is important in relation to his evidence. He gives all the commands relating to sexual mutilation again at that stage when Hrnic has just gone out of the room. So, crucially, in our submission, failing that Fikret/Harambasic test. It is odd that he just puts Dusko Tadic there in the area of the canals, which is probably where he has received some information about events taking place, not doing anything, but is able to identify him, interestingly enough in that half an hour before not being involved with Beganovic or Muslimovic and not identifying anyone else. We say this, it is almost as if there is a sticker with the image of Dusko Tadic and it has been put on the face of the paper. It has that ring about it. We must be clear in our assertions. Plainly, he was emotionally connected with Jasko Hrnic because he is the man who writes 18th June on the wall. Is he now putting that sticker on the picture in that form, not in a detailed form but just as a scrap of information, to stick this on Dusko Tadic? Ferid Mujcic, another one down in the electrical workshop whose evidence was discussed yesterday with the Prosecution and he is also crucial in relation to the chicken kiosk killings, was by the door. He claims that he saw Dusko Tadic behind a guard when the door was opened and Karabasic called out, but Karabasic of course was upstairs, not down in that room. Hrnic was the one called out from that room, not Karabasic. So how reliable is this witness? He told us about his frequent beatings, being the plaything of a particular guard who bullied him all the time and had bullied him on that day. Again, the flavour of his evidence is that he thinks the sexual mutilation victims were Hrnic, Karabasic or Alic, because that is when the sexual language he claims to have heard took place. But we know that the Fikret/Harambasic evidence in fact completely runs contrary to that. So why does a witness such as this give evidence like that, believing or claiming he has seen something? Again, it is the pressure of that room, the circumstances of these men that can well, we say, lead to this kind of thing where a rumour is given subsequently the force of truth. We say that H is far more reliable than a witness such as this. Mehmed Alic who was referred to by me at the time of the leaving of Kozarac and being the only witness on 26th May to see Dusko Tadic at Limenka after the evacuation of people from the town. This is a witness who has the awful tragedy of leading his son out to be mutilated and killed in a savage beating, perhaps. He had to play that role in these events. It is clear that he held back from saying he saw Dusko Tadic. He could not go further than saying: "I know he was there." He added "Dule don't, Dule brother" as being said by one of the victims at the time he was there. In terms of description he said: "I could not see them, who they were, what they were", so he has held back from identifying Dusko Tadic at the scene but, we say, has used for some reason these words as an identifying feature, "Dule don't, Dule brother". Why would that be said then? Is this another example of the nexus being provided in an indirect way? He does that, we say, because he does seek to give responsibility to hold people to account for these events. Interestingly, he puts Dusko Tadic earlier in the day sitting with the Commander of the camp, Meakic. The clear implication to us is that he is trying to hold people responsible for what happened. Interestingly, after he leaves the hangar what was his evidence? It was one perhaps that slipped by most of us as he gave it after he gave the passage, "Dule don't, Dule brother", because he claims that he was taken from the hangar, outside, across the pista to the Camp Commander's office and the camp Commander is informed that Eno Alic has been taken out and "What shall we do with him?" He did not go into the room, so he is holding back from saying that. He was outside and he could hear this being said, "Take him away", meaning Meho Alic, and he is taken all the way back from the administration building back to the red building, the hangar, and back to his room upstairs. That passage is at page 2600 and well worth reading, in our submission, because there is this odd feature of Meakic coming into the account. Why would he be taken by the guard to Meakic's office, the Camp Commander's office and asked "What shall we do with him?" Why? Why would he then be brought back?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not understand. What does this have now to do with the incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Our submission is that he is trying to hold people responsible for his tragedy.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I mean this particular being taken to the Commander's office, what does that have to do with the incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is a very odd feature of his evidence. Our submission is he did not hear "Dule brother" and "Dule don't", and that what he is trying to do is to call people for account.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand that, well it is not important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is odd within the context of these events that he should be taken there and come back. Why would Meakic want to be involved with him at that stage? Why would the guards think that Meho Alic be taken to see the Camp Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What I am saying is what does that have to do with anything? Are you saying he made this up?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: How does that help his position regarding the incident? That is what I do not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is he within the events that he certainly took part in, the taking out of his son, the movement through the hangar, that he is identifying two people and holding them responsible within it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are not following me. It is not important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, I do not understand. It is odd for him to testify he was taken to the Commander's office. What does that do, help his testimony or is that just something odd period?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think our submission is that it has been made up and he is holding the Commander of the camp responsible as well and giving him the knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry if it was not clear. Giving him the knowledge that Eno Alic has been taken out, and pushing responsibility on him in the same way that he has done it on Dusko Tadic by the use of those phrases, "Dule don't, Dule brother." It is a curious piece of evidence and that is our observation upon it. He just said he knew Dusko Tadic was there. He did not see him, he just knew, and he used those words. We say that these are steps being taken by him to hold him responsible. Two other people were involved in the beatings on that afternoon, and I turn to them now, Emir Beganovic who had been beaten several times, within an inch of his life by all accounts, had suffered horrific injuries and was obviously a very brave and strong man to survive what he had to go through. He mentions Dusko Tadic as being part of the group that assaulted him, but does not specifically say what he did. His main attacker is identified as being a man called Dragan who had beaten him on many other occasions, in fact two occasions, on two previous occasions, and had been someone who had been searching for him. In a way this may be significant evidence because he says after he has finished with Beganovic, "Bring me Senad Muslimovic". He is giving orders this man, Dragan. That indeed is what happens, that second victim was brought down that afternoon for the man Dragan and Senad Muslimovic is then beaten, and obviously was specifically required by that person. We have here a witness claiming that Tadic was part of the group of people who took part in this assault, and that he was kicked at the same time as a man called Jasko was also being beaten. So he links these two events, Jasko Hrnic of the three and himself being there at the same time. The Court again will have to look at this evidence to see whether he is a reliable witness. He described being kicked and it is here that the karate kicks are given particular prominence. I have addressed the Court about this feature that most of the witnesses seem to have taken part in karate training, that it does not, on the face of it, establish any particular hallmark by which one could properly identify a person. He was shown a photograph of the Defendant after this trial had started on 9th May, and he did not know Dusko Tadic before. Again, we have this flaw that we say took place in the identification process, four years later after the trial had started. I will not mention the place where he said he lived, but it was discussed yesterday and one would have expected that there had been certainly material from this case that he would have seen and been aware of. Whilst he claims to have been out there in the hangar and Jasko whom he described, with great vividness by the Prosecution yesterday as being sliced by the man in the photograph like chops, none of the calling out process, none of the buildup process, is within his evidence. He says he was being beaten, Tadic was there beating him, and that at the same time as he was being beaten Jasko was being sliced like chops. Well, that is not how those events occurred on that afternoon. We say that this is an example of the rumour mill and perhaps him identifying an assailant incorrectly, and without accuracy that we say the Court should require in relation to these allegations. There are too many flaws and problems within the accounts given for the certainty to get to that level, and that the evidence of H is more than a reasonable doubt in the context of these witnesses. His small voice at that time perhaps was left out in the heat of the desire for revenge to what had happened to those unfortunate men. Your Honour, I finish now with paragraph 6 of the indictment and turn to paragraph 7. Noting the time and feeling quite a dry voice, I wonder if the Court would permit a slightly earlier rise?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess until 2.30. 12.55 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We had set aside two days with a third day if it was needed. Are we going to finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We will certainly finish in the third day, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Today is Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it? How time flies.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: When you are having fun, as they say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am certainly going to be about another 20 minutes and then Miss de Bertodano will probably be about an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And then Mr. Wladimiroff is going to tell us about 7.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Orie after that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie -- sorry, Mr. Orie.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Slightly under half an hour and then Mr. Wladimiroff to wind up so ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have lost track of those hours now. Let us see. I am trying to figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: About two hours left on this side of the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What about rebuttal? Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: First of all, your Honour we do request that we be allowed to give rebuttal. Secondly, we believe our rebuttal would be no more than two hours, unless there are many questions from the bench.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That will encourage me at least not to ask a question, if you promise two hours! So we will then finish by tomorrow at 1.00. Everyone is nodding their head yes, is that right? Then we will finish at 1.00. Mr. Kay, would you like to continue, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I turn now to paragraph 7 of the indictment and paragraph 10 of the indictment because the witness to both these paragraphs is the same witness, Hase Icic, and I will deal with paragraph 7, first of all, which is the beating of a man called Sefik Sivac when he is thrown into the room in the White House on to the floor and he dies at some stage thereafter. At the time this occurred, this witness claimed to have recognised the throwing into the room of the battered body of Sefik Sivac who died in the night. His evidence was that he recognised Dusko Tadic. Obviously seeing someone is a far more powerful form of identification than identification by hearing a voice in respect of which a number of different cognitive faculties are required. This witness himself had been beaten soon after his arrival at the White House. His evidence was that he could not, in fact, recognise his old friend and cousin, Sefik Sivac, who had been thrown into the room and was next to him until it was light and daylight came into the room because, as we know, there was no electricity in this room. His evidence was that Dusko Tadic did not come into the room but was in the doorway and the only lighting occurred outside that room from some form of generator that had been rigged up to illuminate the hallway. We point out to the Court that in his statement of February 1993 he said that he did not identify the accused by sight but by voice, and there has been a significant change in the way he claims to have recognised this witness and come to this Court to tell us about it. I repeat what I said about the difference in recognition between voice and sight, one being, we would say, far more accurate than the other. During his evidence this witness had questions asked of him by me concerning the name Dule. I raise this matter now as it might also be a feature of evidence within paragraph 6 that the Court might like to consider, because he had made a statement referring to one Dusan Knezevic or Dusko Knezevic -- Dusan Knezevic -- and used the name "Dule" in respect of him. We have heard of other Dule's in evidence. I think the accused referred to Dule Jankovic, the deputy Commander of police in Prijedor. Charge 10, paragraph 10, of the indictment which concerns his evidence as well is his own beating in the White House where this room at the end of the corridor seems to have been erected or used as some form of torture chamber or beating chamber by guards in relation to people held in that building. Again, he is the sole witness on the matter, but we do point out to the Court that on 8th July 1992 this is an occasion when the police duty states, the record of duty for Dusko Tadic does have an impact upon one of the charges because it shows that he was on duty at Orlovci between 7 o'clock in the morning to 7 o'clock in the evening. That we can pray in aid here and remarks will be addressed to you by Miss de Bertodano concerning our view of that piece of the Defence evidence which reveals his whereabouts as an essential part of his alibi. But a significant feature we say about the unreliability of this witness is the way he was prepared to change his evidence from voice recognition which he had said in a statement to facial recognition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That statement was a very special sort of statement, was it not? It was written by him almost on medical advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: In order to clear his mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: What, however, at the date when it was written was known generally in the media or elsewhere about the name Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think we have had evidence that by that stage there had already been a programme on German television at about that time in 1993. Someone will correct me. It is something that I had forgotten, he actually features in the film of Monika Gras, this particular ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic does?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- witness himself -- no, this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: This witness, but does the Monika Gras post date or ante date his statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I make an enquiry about that, your Honour, as I cannot recollect?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The statement was before the indictment was issued, that is for sure. I think it was in January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am told it may well be later.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Which is later?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The film.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is something perhaps we can better check out by looking at the evidence to assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: If you discover anything, you might let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We will, but it is an interesting move from sight in this courtroom and previously the identification had been voice. Whatever explanation one gives, it is the actual means of recognition which is so very different, particularly given the statement that the body in the room was not recognised by him although it was his old friend and cousin. But there we have it. There is this move, and it is another indicator to us of where witnesses will be prepared to move in relation to the quality of the evidence they give, as we say it, in an endeavour to pin this defendant.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Did not Mr. Icic testify that he in a statement -- he testified that he saw Mr. Tadic and another man throwing in Mr. Sivac, and he could tell that because of the light coming from the hallway. Then you are saying that the statement that he wrote, and it was before the indictment, on the advice of a physician because he had no one to talk to ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- in the area where he was. In the statement he said that he heard Mr. Tadic and he testified, though, that the reason that he recognised his voice is that he had heard him the night before when he was being beaten when he walked in and was face to face with Mr. Tadic. Is that not sufficient? He also knew Mr. Tadic. Is that not sufficient identification, is that your position, or is it your position that in addition to the voice when he testifies he says that he saw him?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It certainly can be. I am not saying that voice recognition is impossible, but it is a move that the witness has made. So if one accepts that he is not being frank with the Court about the visual recognition, that it is a case of him believing voice recognition, he has rather cut off that path by denying that and moving that by preventing, perhaps, exploration of those issues. That is where the unreliability of the evidence, perhaps, is best to be seen.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He has cut off the path for visual identification because he did not mention that when he wrote it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For voice recognition, why it was that he recognised the voice. He is staying with visual recognition, and that is what he maintained in this courtroom. One has to remember the circumstances in which he was held and whether that would be good enough with all those men and bodies in that room, the throwing in of the body into the room, whether that would be sufficient in those circumstances for which an accurate and correct voice identification could be made.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: When he testified, it was his position that he heard him and saw him?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you recall how long that statement was? The statement was not admitted but, as I read through the transcript, he was on page 4. You asked him to go to page 4 to look for his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So can I assume it was a four-page statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour is testing me here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is only because I have read it more recently -- well, I do not know when you read it. I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is a stamped page 200, but it was certainly not a 200 page statement.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, I saw that too. No, he said that he had written the statement out and it did not contain everything that had happened to him but he just wanted to get some things off

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So when you pointed him to page 4, I assumed it was a four-page statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, it was more than a four-page statement.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: As I said, you pointed him to page 4 to look at his signature. Therefore, I assumed that if he saw his signature on page 4 his statement could not have been any longer than four pages. That was my only question. I think it is correct because I read it last week. I am not relying on something that happened four years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, but he did identify the document with his signature on which was, presumably, the purpose of that. He described, as I recollect it, and what was put to him in that statement when he used the word "Dule" in relation to Duca Knezevic as being a slip of the pen. Moving now to paragraph 8 of the indictment, this is the killing of a number of named individuals but the most particular one with which we are concentrating in relation to evidence is Salih Elezovic. The 27th July 1992 has been supplied as the date through the witness Ermin Strikovic and a time of 14.20 p.m., because in his account someone told him that time when that man left his room which was in the middle section of the rooms on the first floor of the White House. To a certain extent, we are relying on the accuracy of that other person's timing and date and, if it is right, obviously, whatever happened would have happened after that particular time. This was a particular day that Dusko Tadic was on duty at Orlovci between 1900 hours and 7 o'clock in the morning of the next day. This count really starts in its investigation with the ownership of those shoes of Salih Elezovic which are a key feature of the evidence. These were worn by Samir Hodzic, one of the two witnesses to the material facts in relation to the matters alleged here, because he took them off the body of Salih Elezovic and to have done that he plainly had contact with Salih Elezovic. Our submission is the Court can accept that he would have had dealings on that occasion with that body to come into ownership and possession of the shoes. Any other explanation would probably be unreasonable. He was turning over those bodies, as the Court discussed yesterday during the Prosecution submissions, for a purpose of identification or whatever reason, but for some reason he was turning them over, and in the collection of bodies that he saw was this Salih Elezovic. The other witness on the matter, Hakija Elezovic, gives a very different account to Samir Hodzic to what had taken place behind the White House and the interaction of these two witnesses. Samir Hodzic gave evidence that on that afternoon, although he was in the White House with Hakija Elezovic, before he saw those bodies near the White House he was taken out and he never saw Hakija Elezovic again after Hakija Elezovic had been taken for interrogation. He did not see Hakija Elezovic behind the White House, nor did he ask him if he could have the shoes of his son Salih. As I said, Samir Hodzic had those shoes and so it would be right to accept his explanation as to how he came into possession of them, that he did take them off one of the bodies. So with the trail concerning the evidence starting there, what does he say about the man he alleges was Dusko Tadic who was present at the scene? He described him as having a facial irritation, some form of sun tan, with no beard and light hair which was high on his forehead. We say how could that possibly be a right and accurate description of Dusko Tadic? Hakija ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Was that his testimony or was that the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That was his evidence as well as in his statement.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, and he adhered to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The reason why we mention it is because he was trying to move from lightish to black and it simply did not make sense. For whatever reason he was trying to give an explanation about that. The Prosecution did not, in fact, ask him for this description. It came through in cross-examination. It may well be they were aware of the risks to them in relation to this count. But Hakija Elezovic claimed to have seen Dusko Tadic at the time of a mass beating and killing behind the White House at which he saw Tadic beating his son and Tadic also beat him, but for some reason he miraculously survived. If the object was to kill those men, we say, well, it seems odd that he was allowed to survive if the purpose was killing and nothing was done about him. But he says that he saw Samir Hodzic behind the White House with an Albanian loading bodies and there were some 50 or 60 near lifeless or lifeless bodies around, not the picture that Hodzic who got those shoes describes. He described seeing Samir Hodzic take the shoes off the body and he said to him that he could have them, and that the two of them walked back together into the White House, returned together and were in that building at the same time. I point out to the Court that that is at great variance with Hodzic's own evidence that he returned on his own, he ran back to the White House because a guard told him to scram, he was on his own and he was carrying the shoes in his hand. The pictures between the two men are entirely different, and this is a great problem in relation to this evidence. One witness has had extreme misfortune and the loss of a son and claims that he was there at the killing of that son by Tadic. But the accounts are at great variance. Our submission is that it may well have occurred from Samir Hodzic's misidentification, as it was a misidentification, in his evidence and statement about the description of the man he claimed was Tadic, that somehow gave this connection to the other man Hakija Elezovic in relation to the allegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am sorry. I do not follow what you have just said; would you rephrase it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I will try. These people left Omarska, they went to various camps. Hodzic was a relative of Elezovic. Although he claimed not to have seen him again, one thing is for sure, he had those shoes and they came into his possession that way. It may well be, as we say, that he made a misidentification that fed itself back, either directly or indirectly, to the other man and by that means he made the allegation that he saw Tadic killing his son and he was there and described a scene that was not the scene taking place. Hodzic did not say that there were 50 or 60 bodies behind the White House. There is the issue as to whether he looked. His first answer to the Prosecution's question was "I would have known what was behind the White House". He was then asked, "Well, did you look?" and he said, no, but he would have been aware. We are not talking here about a big building, we are talking about a very small building, and him particularly being on the side or towards the corner of it. 50 or 60 bodies would be hardly something you would miss behind there. They would not all be stacked up out of his angle of view, particularly if what was being described was happening as the witness Elezovic said. It is difficult for us to explain this, but there is this enormous contradiction between the two witnesses. The witness Elezovic also claims Tadic beat him during an interrogation in Keraterm. The only allegation we have heard of Dusko Tadic being present during an interrogation in Keraterm comes from this witness, from his own interrogation which took place, he said, with the questions being asked by a man called Radakovic who was the director of the National Park of Kozara. He, apparently, also interviewed him at Omarska. Again it is a feature that has come through to us rather like it did with the Meho Alic point that we made and we ask the Court to consider, of this trying to make people responsible for something. It seems odd to us that there would be that same interrogator at Keraterm, meeting him at Omarska, Tadic is also at Keraterm, Tadic is at Omarska. We say this is, perhaps, an attempt to pin responsibility for what happened upon this accused. There are other contradictions. Elezovic says that a man called Turkanovic was in the pile of dead, whereas Samir Hodzic said quite clearly that he was alive when he returned to the room in the White House, that that is where that person was, and he died subsequently when he was taken out of the room.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Kay, did Mr. Hodzic know Mr. Tadic prior to this incident? I do not recall. I have not read that testimony for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Did he know, I mean, knew him -- what was the relationship?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He went to his cafe. He did not socialise with him, but he knew him in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You say that Hodzic and Elezovic were related, and if it was their goal to manufacture this and blame it on the accused, well, why would Mr. Hodzic then give this identification that you say is wrong, the light to dark?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is very difficult for us to explain that, why stories are not straight and the same. They just come out as being entirely different. We rely on Hodzic as telling the truth about this. In our submissions we are not criticising him. What we are saying is he has misidentified Tadic quite clearly in that description and the key is the shoes. He has the shoes. What he describes happening is very much at variance with the father's account who has a miraculous survival in relation to those events when it seems the object was the killing of all the people.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What I meant -- I probably did not make myself clear -- was if he knew what Mr. Tadic looked like and he is attempting to hold Mr. Tadic responsible, why did he not identify him more closely to what you would view of identification in the statement. You cannot answer the question but ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I simply cannot explain, but the fact of that remains. We simply cannot explain why that would happen but it just has.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He identified him by name as well as describing his hair colour?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, and the description, not only of the hair colour, but the high forehead.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Of course, now the Prosecutor said, I believe, in their closing argument that Mr. Elezovic had lost two sons and that would explain his confusion about whether he had given shoes to Mr. Hodzic and also whether he had actually seen Mr. Hodzic load bodies, as opposed to just seeing him turn them over. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A confused witness probably does not help their case and that is a problem for them, because we need reliable witnesses and in his confusion we say he is wrong about Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have not read this recently but, as I recall, Mr. Elezovic testified that he knew Mr. Tadic through his son; it was one of his sons who really knew Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have not checked to see whether he actually saw him, but my impression was that he kind of knew what he looked like, but there had not been a close relationship. It was one of his sons who was his associate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. He said he knew him by sight and it was, in fact, Salih who is dead and the subject of this charge was the one that Dusko Tadic knew. But there is that feature, as I said, of the interrogator being the same in the two places and Tadic being present at his interrogation in Keraterm for no apparent reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Before you leave the old fisherman Elezovic, he, I think, is almost the only witness who tells us where north is in relation to Omarska which, in fact, if one is going to ever describe Omarska, is very important. Can you confirm that the Omarska hangar runs north-south? That is my understanding from Elezovic, but I do not know if you know of any other evidence as to its position?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I was trying to think whether we have a plan of Omarska with north-south on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I do not think so, not that I have seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I cannot remember that, your Honour. Your Honour is quite right when he referred to east, west, north south which, for the rest of us, perhaps, took us by surprise in following which direction he was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, but I do see nods from the Prosecution. Can I assume that it runs north-south?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think that probably helps all of us.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: While we are talking about Omarska, I had looked on this list -- if you are finished with 15 through 17 -- and I do not think I see the distance from Omarska town to the camp. Did we hear that it was three kilometres or two kilometres? Can you at some point, the Prosecution and the Defence, give us a stipulation or add it to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am sure we will; we have all done it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It may be on here. I just need to spend more time looking at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We had difficulty trying to locate it on the map with witnesses. He referred to the driving of the truck around when Hodzic was there by the Albanian at the time of moving the bodies -- at great variance with what Hodzic describes. Now moving, in fact, to the last count that I have to deal with on the indictment, and this is the count dealing with abuse of prisoners and the fire extinguisher allegation, again a single witness count being that of Elvir Grozdanic. The description of his evidence given through the demonstrative aids by the Prosecution during their closing address supports the Defence contention that the abuse of the prisoners by asking them to drink water from puddles, jumping on their backs and beating them, which was taking place in front of the White House involving the man Knezevic and Jovic, was actually not a feature of the evidence in relation to this allegation that involved Dusko Tadic. He was seen separately and further up towards the administration building. Your Honours may recollect the plan we looked at yesterday where he had marked the various sightings and how, in fact, Tadic on his account was walking away to where the bins were in the direction of the administration building. So that is the first point we make about this particular allegation. The account given by Grozdanic, who again was a witness who believed that Tadic was looking for him but around and about in this area at the time, we say, because we criticise his testimony, cannot be right if that was so; that if Tadic was looking for him, given what he says about him, that he would have been in great peril then. There is this issue over whether the inhumane treatment can apply to a corpse. There is no evidence that the recipient of the fire extinguisher was alive or dead. It is with no satisfaction that we make observations on allegations such as this, but we are bound to do it. He described the body as being finished with and past its use from abuse that had taken elsewhere. In those circumstances, with the body being put in the wheelbarrow, we say there is more of an indication that that was a corpse being wheeled away than a human being in living form.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, there is no evidence, as I recall, that the fire extinguisher was discharged. The indictment in paragraph 9 charges that it was discharged. Does that make a difference? So that if there is no proof that it was discharged and the only proof is it was put in someone's mouth, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am just looking up my trial notes on the point, your Honour, and I thought he did give evidence that it was discharged -- oh, he did not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have not read it recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "Putting the fire hose into the mouth of the man being wheeled away", that was how it was put. The Court will obviously be considering this particular allegation within the framework, whether it does come up to that level as required legally to constitute ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- the offence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: My question really is a matter of the law. When it is charged that the fire extinguisher was discharged, and that is at variance with the evidence, what is the consequence of that, from your point of view?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just putting it in, not sufficient, we would say, in the context of this kind of case. Perhaps a more grave form of the discharging of it would certainly be if it was on a living person. The release of the foam from the fire extinguisher would, obviously, be an abuse of prisoner. Putting it into the mouth as he described ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: I think what he said was that it was shoved into the mouth of the .....

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are still not answering my question. My question is, if it is charged that it was discharged and there is no evidence (and I am not certain; my recollection is that there was no evidence of that), is that a significant variance? What is the legal consequence, if you can ---

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Oh, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- tell me that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Say it if you feel that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am grateful for your Honour spotting something that certainly I had not, because I was working off the words of the indictment and it had not come certainly to me -- probably to others but not to me -- about just the shoving in of the mouth. That is not sufficient, in our submission, to constitute sufficient abuse in relation to this count; discharging would and the evidence has not come up to proof on that feature. So, the round of our submission is that legally none of it satisfies this particular charge on the indictment. I do not know whether your Honours have any further questions of me? I have been 45 minutes instead of half an hour, but that is the full extent of my submissions upon the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Much has been said by Prosecution witnesses about the fear which the name "Dule" inspired and by the presence of Tadic apparently in the camp. Can you explain why there was this fear?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It could well derive from that spark that we say was hit by G in June, on 18th June, and that is why we say rumour began to give the form of truth. That was certainly the most horrific day that we have heard about in the evidence. Until that time days were bad enough, but what we have heard on that particular day taking place after the camp had been opened, let us say, some 20 days, and if he hit that spark that caused that rumour, one is not surprised that there would be that fear and trepidation. The problem is if he is wrong. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Just taking up that very interesting question from Judge Vohrah, nothing that we have heard of the accused's time before the war in Kozarac would give rise to any fear of him at all, I imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Therefore, when you do hear of this fear, one has to see some reason for it as at the time that it is expressed. One finds that only in actions after the war, presumably in the camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, there are other Dule's, as I pointed out earlier this afternoon in my submission. Dule is not an exclusive badge of this defendant. When I opened my address to the Court, I referred to the bogey man figure that Tadic seemed to have become. Perhaps he was a powerful man, a big man, from a traditional family with a father held in a certain esteem. But there was that bogey man feature that was there, we would say, before the conflict and that continued which is why we chose that phrase in the camp. There were other Dule's. There is no doubt about that. But once rumour goes round these unfortunate places and the pressure and intensity by which these people passed their lives, we can understand what would happen in relation to a misidentification becoming gradually stronger and stronger. People lend their names eventually to sign up to these matters.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Did we not have testimony -- at least I think the Prosecution made reference to testimony from one witness who said that Emir Karabasic had said that, "If Dule finds out I am here, then I am in trouble because I know too much"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that a possible reason, if you accept that, for there to be fear at least in Emir's mind or Mr. Karabasic's mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That was the witness Seferovic, the man with the birds, the orchard, and the sleighing of the two policemen, Osman and Edin Besic. It is a rather interesting remark because it rather implies that Tadic had not been in the camp before that day, if that is so, so it does not quite fit the matrix of the Prosecution case. One would have expected from the profile they presented that he would have known that he was there if he was part of the selecting of police officers or targeting individuals, he would certainly have known where, if that was the case, that there was to be this conflict and killing of Karabasic, that would have been something he would have known about before.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you whether the evidence indicated what date Mr. Karabasic was placed in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I do not think we have had evidence about that other than the fact that the policemen formed the head of the convoy from Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not remember any. My last question that relates to these questions is what effect do you feel the intensity, if that is the word to use for these events, the horrific nature, as you have described them, of these events, what effect does that have on a person's ability to recall with precision some of the details as opposed to identifying the person?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Some say that it is for ever printed on your memory.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The identity of the person or what happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The events that you never forget. We certainly do not have consistencies of account.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We should have asked Dr. Wagenaar that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That would have been one that would have helped us, at least his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Can I deal with your Honour's earlier point about Karabasic? He had been in for some time. You will recollect that he was known within that end room on the first floor and that he had been there for some time. He had already been interrogated and beaten. I think we can take it he had been there for quite some time. He was not a fresh arrival or anything like that; the evidence indicates otherwise.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you recall what is the first date of an allegation that Mr. Tadic was in the Omarska camp? This would have been the first of the substantive counts, but there may be a date in count 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As I recollect it, early June on the pista but, your Honour, if I can just check this?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before June 18th?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I think, in fact, it is 29th May and it is Hamdija Kahrimanovic, and I am right on this. It is not a question of "think", it is right. 29th May, 4.00 to 5 o'clock, when he was on the pista.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: What was the name of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Hamdija Kahrimanovic, pages 2100 to 2138. He was in Omarska for a short period of time from 27th May to 5th June and he claims to have seen him as well on 4th to 5th June at about midday in the same place. To put him in context, he was one of the League of Peace delegation from Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss de Bertodano, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I am to address you on the Defence case. The way I intend to do it is to first go through the alibi and then make some observations on the previous statements made by Mr. Tadic both in his interviews and in the work report which he wrote. Before I start, there are two very general points that I would like to make about the difficulties that have been attendant on this defence. The first one was mentioned already yesterday which is that this defence relates to a period of over six months and we are providing an alibi defence. This is not an alibi which says, "I was in the United States of America during this time". It is an alibi which says, "I was living in the area but I did not do the offences with which I am charged". The difficulty about that is that one is never going to get to a situation where you have witnesses who can cover every minute of what the defendant was doing over this kind of period of time and, although some of the allegations in the indictment are linked to specific dates, many of them have really no date at all. So that is a difficulty in this kind of case, and one which is not of the defendant's making. The second difficulty (which I will not dwell on and which you know of already) is the difficulty we have had in the course of our investigations. First, in finding the people who will speak to us and, secondly, even if they do speak to us, in persuading them to come and give evidence before this Tribunal, whether by video link or in The Hague. I think we can safely say that we have not had all the witnesses that we would like to have had appearing for the Defence. However, what we have produced is a series of witnesses who have spoken about their dealings with Dusko Tadic over this period of some six months and who have confirmed, we say, as far as is reasonably possible the story that he has given right from the start. In general, people spend a great deal of time with their family, so it is of no surprise that the witnesses Mira Tadic, Dusko Tadic's wife, and his brother Ljubomir cover substantial parts of this alibi. On top of this, we have managed to produce concrete documentary evidence which supports again the story given by the defendant right from the start showing that he worked in the police during the months of June, July, August up to September, and these documents confirm what he has always said to be the case. Moreover, they do give what we would not otherwise have, specific times at which he was at a certain place. I shall say more about these later. We are not required to prove our alibi in any way. What we are required to do is to cast reasonable doubt on the Prosecution evidence. In our submission, we have succeeded in more than doing that. We have provided the Court with a detailed chronological schedule of alibi which takes the Court through day by day as to what Dusko Tadic was doing, and which witnesses back this up. I do not intend to go through this page by page or day by day. What I intend to do is take you through the general story and look at the witnesses who have come to give evidence in support of that story. The history of the accused's movements at this time starts in April when his family move from Kozarac, as do other families in the town, because of the rising tensions in the area. The Tadic family, we have heard, left the town for a substantial part of April and went to stay in Kozice. Dusko himself, however, returned to live and work in Kozarac. The family returned just before the end of the month in the belief that the situation had calmed down. Ironically, soon after that Prijedor was taken over by the Serbs and the family then had to leave again. It has been alleged by the Prosecution that this was no coincidence, that this can be seen as evidence that Dusko Tadic knew that the takeover of Prijedor was going to happen. We say the opposite is the case. Had he known, why would the family immediately afterwards have left again? In any case, had he known, surely, it would have been obvious to anyone that if Prijedor was taken over by Serb control, the situation in Kozarac, the Muslim stronghold, was likely to get more difficult and more tense rather than less so. In any case, as the defendant remarked to his brother Ljubo at the time, it was a case of "Here we go again" and off the family went to Banja Luka in the car of the local priest. Having arrived in Banja Luka, they obtained the house in Starcevica. We have seen photos of it in Exhibit 62. They obtained this with the help of Ljubo's friend, Nedim Alic. So begins nearly two months of residence in Banja Luka. Dusko Tadic, of course, did not stay in Banja Luka during this time. He still had his business in Kozarac to run. So, having settled his family in, he then returned to Kozarac to look after the cafe. At about this time as well, and we suggest with even greater irony in view of the allegations that are being made, Ljubomir opens up a new business in Kozarac, a discount drinks store, right next to Dusko Tadic's cafe. He only opens it up at the beginning of May. He receives a substantial delivery of beer on 21st May, only to find on 22nd that he can no longer return to Kozarac. We suggest, of course, that had Dusko Tadic known anything of what was going to happen, he would have at least suggested to his brother that this was not the time to be starting up a business and certainly would have told him to stop receiving deliveries at a time when the Prosecution allege Dusko Tadic knew exactly what was going to happen on 24th May. On 23rd May, after the blockade of Kozarac had started, Dusko Tadic leaves Kozarac, and he leaves in the car of Trivo Reljic who has come to give evidence. Again it has been suggested that he left on 23rd because he knew what was going to happen. Mr. Kay touched on this yesterday. Everyone knew that something was going to happen. All the Serbs were leaving Kozarac. Many Muslims who had the opportunity to leave were leaving as well. We have heard from Kemal Susic that he himself said to Sejad Cirkin on 23rd May, "There is no way out for us", meaning of the conflict, "There is no way of escaping that", and he added in his evidence, "And we all knew that." The cite for that is page 2186. So, what we have here is a situation where everyone knew, everyone had heard, everyone saw what was happening. One did not have to be told of the plans by those who intended to attack Kozarac to decide that the best option was to leave. So, we have a picture of this family who is not a family privy to any special knowledge about what is going on at this stage. It is a family which is fleeing, not fighting.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, but if everyone knew that this was going to happen, then Mr. Ljubomir Tadic perhaps made the decision to go ahead in the face of that information.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: I am not saying, your Honour, that everyone knew there was going to be a massive shelling of Kozarac, only that everyone could see ---

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That it was coming to a head.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: --- the situation was becoming untenable.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sure. You had April 29th -- was it April 29th -- that Prijedor was taken over.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: April 30th that Prijedor was taken over.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: April 30th it was taken over, so that was a month before.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is becoming awfully close.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: We suggest this was a period when tensions were building up. We have the meetings of the Peace League which Kemal Susic and Hamdija Kahrimanovic had talked about as well as Dusko Tadic. I think that Kemal Susic's remarks were made in the light of the situation that the Peace Council was seen to have failed, that until that time, I believe (although I am saying this off the top of my head), the second meeting of the Peace League was somewhere about May 20th, until that time it may be that there was still considerable hope that fighting in Kozarac could be averted. After this, we get into the serious ultimatums being made and we have heard that from 22nd May there was actually a blockade of Kozarac. That was the situation which everyone saw themselves in. This had not happened before 22nd May, so to leave first thing on 23rd May does not seem to me to be an extraordinary coincidence. We have heard also from Prosecution witnesses -- I mention Husein Hodzic -- that Dusko Tadic left on that day. I think there is little dispute that that happened. We have heard from Jelena Gajic that he came to her apartment in Prijedor before taking a train to Banja Luka. Then we have heard from Ljubo Tadic that he arrived in Banja Luka that afternoon. More importantly, perhaps, we have heard evidence from witness X who is the [redacted] who came to give evidence. She said that when the Tadic family arrived in Banja Luka, they came to her house that evening and she was very specific that it was that evening and they stayed the night in her house. The Prosecution suggested yesterday that it is very unlikely that someone would remember that with such certainty after all this time. Our submission is that it is not at all unlikely because one of the reasons why witnesses remember dates or remember specific incidents is because they link them with other important incidents. Witness X testified that she heard soon after about the attack on Kozarac. It seems clear to me that, being a friend of Dusko Tadic, having seen him on the night that he fled from Kozarac, that would be linked very clearly in her mind with hearing that the day after that Kozarac was shelled. Having arrived in Banja Luka, Dusko Tadic stays in that house in Starcevica until 15th June. We have many witnesses who have testified that they saw him regularly in Banja Luka during that time. We have heard from Dragoje Balta who was his next door neighbour in Koste Jarica Street. He came and gave evidence that Dusko had been his neighbour during this time; that they had met several times and, indeed, that they had spent a considerable amount of time in each other's company. This man was an ordinary locksmith. He did not know Dusko Tadic. He was not an old friend of his. He has no apparent reason for coming to The Hague and giving that evidence, unless it is true. I recall when he was giving the testimony in cross-examination that there were some attempts to paint him in a sort of sinister light because he had been part of a rather, well, perhaps you could call it a sort of Dad's Army guarding some buildings nearby for a purpose which he said he had never found out. We would suggest that that was laughable. We then heard from Nikola Petrovic. He said that he saw the accused on 24th May and every two to three days thereafter. We have heard from Borka Rakic, Witness X, again testifying they had seen Dusko Tadic often during this period. Witness D testified that when she first saw the family in Prijedor afterwards, they told her that they had been in Banja Luka all that time. So, although during this period we cannot give concrete evidence of every date, we cannot say he had lunch with so and so on that day and supper with so and so. What we can provide is a body of witnesses all of whom saw him often in Banja Luka dressed in civilian clothes behaving in an ordinary manner. During this period until 15th June we have heard that Dusko Tadic left Banja Luka on three occasions. The first time we have heard is about 1st June when, having heard that the fighting is more or less over in Kozarac, he goes back with his brother Ljubo to see that his property is still intact. He goes on a similar visit on 8th or 9th June and on this occasion he stays the night. On both these occasions he travels by train to Omarska. He walks to the house of Milenko Timarac, his friend and former waiter. Milenko Timarac provides the transport for them to go to Kozarac. On each of these occasions they stay in Kozarac for no more than a couple of hours. On the second occasion they hire a truck to get them back because they are taking their possessions with them. The third occasion on which he left Banja Luka was on 6th June when he and Jovo Samardzija visited the collection centre at Trnopolje. We have heard from Jovo Samardija. He said that Dusko Tadic was asked by him to go with him to help him find his sister, Dara, whom he thought might be in Trnopolje camp. We have heard that Dusko Tadic was reluctant to go, but that he agreed because this was an old man, he could not go alone and he needed help. We have heard they travelled by train to Trnopolje. They stayed for some two hours in the area of the camp. Their search having been unsuccessful, they returned to Banja Luka that afternoon. It was suggested yesterday that the evidence of Jovo Samardzija was in conflict with that of Dusko Tadic; that Jovo Samardzija said that Dusko Tadic spent his whole time with the guards and did not talk to the prisoners. If one checks the transcript of that, that is a misrepresentation of what was, in fact, said. It is certainly true that Mr. Samardzija said that Dusko Tadic talked to the guards. He made no comment on whether he talked to the prisoners or not. But what he did say was, "We were together the whole time". It seems to me that the suggestion from that is that if Mr. Samardija was among the prisoners and he and the defendant were together the whole time, there is no conflict with the story of Mr. Tadic that he spoke to the prisoners as well perhaps as to the guards. I think Mr. Kay mentioned yesterday that this we see as an important recorded visit. It is one that the accused has always said that he made, and it is one in which there is no indication that he had any powers in Trnopolje, that he had any status, that he could order anyone to do anything. He simply is taken along as someone younger, stronger and fitter who can assist this old man in finding his sister. These three are the only occasions on which Dusko Tadic left Banja Luka during this period. Both his brother Ljubomir and his wife Mira, whom we say are the only people in a position to say this, say that he did not leave at any other time. His more casual acquaintances may or may not know that, but the evidence of his brother and his wife is that these are the only visits he made. In each of these cases we have heard from the companion he was with at the time as to exactly what happened on these visits. If I move on now to 15th June, this is the date at which Dusko Tadic returns to Prijedor to join the traffic police. We have heard that he worked there from 16th June up till early August. During this time he stayed first with his cousin Radovan Vokic, then with a Croat family, Martin and Mileva Dzaja, and on a couple of occasions when his duties permitted it he returned to stay with his family in Banja Luka where he still had all his possessions and was still, essentially, based at the time. On 27th June the family moved into a flat in the Pecani apartment blocks and they lived there for the remainder of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me. Let me ask you a question before 27th. In your alibi, the chronology of alibi, you say that from June 15th -- 16th is the first night that Mr. Tadic spends with the Dzaja's, is it?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That is right, yes, that was the evidence that on the night of 15th.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Oh, 15th.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Sorry, I am in July.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, June 15th.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: On the night of 15th he stayed with Radovan Vokic. Then from 16th he stayed with the Dzaja's.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, he goes home and he spends the night with his wife.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: I am sorry, yes, and then we have him staying with the Dzaja's after that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So my question is you have him staying with the Dzaja's for several nights, the 17th, 18th, 19th ----

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, the nights which he was not in Banja Luka ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- 20th, 21st. OK. I went to the transcript that you cited and, as I recall, Mr. Tadic said that he spent several nights. I remember he begins a discussion on the left-hand side of the page. That is all I know and I do not know the page. It is 2000 something. What is it? Anyway, he does not give dates. He does not say that he spent every night that he was in Banja Luka with the Dzaja's. He says that the first night he spent with his wife on the 17th, he said Mrs. Tadic, his wife, spent the night with him. The other nights he spent on his own, but earlier he just said "several". I do not see ----

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: The implication being still with the Dzaja family and this is confirmed in some of the interviews as well. Where he has not said otherwise ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You assume he spent the night?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That is the implication. When he says "alone", he was not sleeping on the streets. He was still staying with the Dzaja family and he is saying "alone" in relation to Mira being there.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: My question really went to whether there is any indication in the transcript that Mr. Tadic said that every night that he was in Banja Luka before they moved into the house on 27th he spent with the Dzaja's. That was really my question.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: I am not sure that he said that in terms, but he says -- in fact, I have it here -- "I slept at Martin and Mileva Dzaja's place" -- this is 6001 -- "for a couple of nights. I do not remember exactly how many. The first time with my wife when we came to Prijedor. After that I spent several nights at their place on my own". That is the bit that you were referring to. We hear later that he moves into Pecani on 27th, but he does not give any other place that he stayed. So we assume that the "several nights" refer to the nights when he is not in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: I might remind the Court that the Dzaja's are two of the witnesses whom we were unable to get to come to The Hague to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I heard several times that they were old and sick. I thought that was reason.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That is right, yes. I was not suggesting that it was for political reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So on 16th, though, he goes home, is that correct? He spends the night at home on 16th?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: In Banja Luka, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then he comes back on 17th ----

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- on the train with his wife?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That was at 6 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: He takes the early train.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What time did that leave?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: He may say in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 6 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: But I think he said it was 6.00 or before 6.00 -- 6 o'clock rings a bell -- and then is on duty on an early shift.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He is supposed to start at 7 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But the train ride is an hour-and-a-half, according to the witness, we heard. So he must have been late then to work on 17th.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: I am trying to find the place in the transcript where he speaks of this.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think he said he left at 6 o'clock and then the other witness, the gentleman who testified via video link, had said that the train ride was an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Yes, but the cite I have here simply says: "So we arrived very early by train from Banja Luka" and does not give a specific time.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think it was Mrs. Tadic who testified that it was 6 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That it was the 6 o'clock train.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So, really, if he arrived at 7.30, then he was on duty at 7.00, and then I went back and looked at the spreadsheet to see if it had indicated that he was late and it did not.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: What I would say is that her getting perhaps the train time wrong by a few minutes or half an hour, it may be that the train left earlier than 6 o'clock. I would have thought it unlikely that she could remember at this stage the exact time at which the train left. What we do not have in evidence ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: She remembered a lot of dates so, I mean .....

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I thought she said before 6.00 but I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: I have 6.00 in my mind; whether she said before 6.00 or at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We do not want to use a lot of time. We will recess for 20 minutes and then we can check the transcripts. Yes, Miss de Bertodano, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: I am sorry, I thought you said we would recess NOW.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I said we would recess at 4.00 and we will have 20 minutes to look at the transcript and then we can come back and talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Just touching then briefly on this flat in Pecani that they moved into, we have had a lot of people, well, a lot of remarks, might I say then, made by the Prosecution that this was a very luxurious flat to get. It is the flat of the old police Commander, Hasan Talundzic. In the context of that, I would like to draw the Court's attention to the photo we have in evidence at D67 of the outside view of the flat where we can see -- this was shown to us by Nada Vlacina who also lived in Pecani -- it actually occupies one window of the third floor of this apartment block, and that the rebuttal witness who was the relation of Talundzic and spoke about the flat said that it had two bedrooms. So just to keep this in perspective, we are not talking about a palatial apartment. We have also had evidence that it was sparsely and poorly furnished from Nada Vlacina. I am turning now to the police duties, and until 1st August which covers a crucial period of this evidence and a period in which the most serious allegations have been made, Dusko Tadic was working almost every day at the traffic checkpoint at Orlovci. On 3rd August, also in the traffic police, he worked one shift as Most Na Sani. The Court has heard the evidence of many witnesses who saw him regularly at this checkpoint; to mention some, Nada Vlacina, Radoslavka Lukic, Dragolje Jankovic, Rajko Karanovic and Zeljko Maric. Many of these witnesses are ordinary people with nothing to hide, no reason for saying that he was there if he was not. So there can be no doubt that he was, in fact, a reserve policeman at the Orlovci checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I ask you a question with respect to Mr. Jankovic? He testified that he saw Mr. Tadic on duty at the Orlovci checkpoint before Mr. Tadic delivered the goods to his home for storage and that was in May. How could he -----

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: No, no, the goods were delivered to his home sometime in July. I have forgotten the exact date. There are two goods deliveries; the first one on 15th June to the house of Sava Vokic and the second one to the house of Dragolje Jankovic. That is at some date in July.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Maybe we can check the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: I will check that over the break, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I remember asking him when he delivered the goods. He was talking about the attack on Kozarac. We got into a long discussion as to whether or not it was during the shelling or after the shelling. He finally agreed that it was May, I thought, when the goods were delivered the first time.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: I remember the unclarity and my memory of it was it being clarified.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then I asked him, "Well, when did you see Mr. Tadic?" He said, "Before the goods were delivered". So you can check the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: I will check that over the break, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there an indication in the transcript of what hours Miss, what is her name, Vokic, the relative?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Mrs. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
