utterances.text: Is there an indication in the transcript what hours she worked? I know she worked at the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Yes. She was the witness who spoke of a curfew at 9 o'clock in the evening, so we are talking of a time before that, before the curfew. But again I do not recall whether she said exactly what her hours were. My recollection is that she had more than one job during this period and the hours may have differed, but again I can check.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. I thought that she had travelled through the checkpoint on her way to the hotel. I have not gone back to check, but I was just wondering what her hours would have been so we could determine when she would have seen Mr. Tadic in terms of his assignment. The other question relates to

utterances.speaker: MRS. VLACINA
utterances.text: did she testify that she saw him more than once after the first half of June or just during the first half of June?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: She said several times within that period. I do not think she was absolutely specific as to what period, but she had family who lived in Orlovci and whom she went to visit. That is the connection in which she came in contact with him.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am trying to remember. I suppose I am asking you for transcript cites so I will not have to re-read the entire 6,000 pages. We will stand in recess for 20 minutes. 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, before I forget the references that you made to the transcript during your presentation ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- would you please provide citations for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You will get the transcript and then as soon as you can get those to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, if I can look at the transcript to do it as I cannot carry it in my head.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, after you get it back, if you can, as quickly as possible. Miss de Bertodano?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Your Honour, to clear up the three matters that we were discussing before the break, the first time being the time that the Tadics arrived in Prijedor on 16th ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I was asking what time they had left, and I had thought it was 6 a.m. but you tell me.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That is right. In the evidence of Mira Tadic, she says, "On the day after, on 17th, we left for Prijedor together". Question: "What time did you leave for Prijedor?" "Early in the morning, 6 o'clock, I think. I think our train left at 6 o'clock". She does not then give a time of arrival and that is at page 4887. But to cross-reference that with the evidence of Dragoljub Savic, who was the station master, when he was going through the lists of trains he cited one which arrived in Prijedor at 6.42 a.m. That was for 23rd May, but we heard from his evidence that the timetables were regular, so I would suggest that that would be the train that was referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I thought that he had said it was an hour-and-a-half trip, but I have not gone back to his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: This simply says it arrives at Prijedor railway station at 6.42. I cannot trace when it leaves Banja Luka, but in any case the page reference is 5350 for that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: The second point related to the evidence of Dragolje Jankovic and time when the goods were left at his flat. Your Honour was quite right in her recollection that when asked, "Do you recollect when that was?" he says, "I do not remember the exact date but it was in May". That is at page 5526. There is then some further questions to pin down this time in relation to the conflict in Kozarac. He says this is while the conflict was still ongoing. It then becomes clear, turning over to 5527, that when he talks of the conflict he is not talking about the shelling which he says lasted for three days at the beginning of the conflict, but talking, apparently, about that whole time period. That is at page 5527. That has come back to in re-examination at 5534. The depositing of goods is said to be at a time after he was in the police. That is the closest we can get on his evidence to giving it a date. It is not entirely satisfactory for the Defence purposes, but it is clear from his evidence it was while what he calls the conflict was going on, not three days, but the ensuing events. He says that is sometime in May. We know that cannot be right. He is not specific about a date, but he does say that it was after Dusko Tadic started working at Orlovci checkpoint. That is well documented as being 16th June. So I am afraid that is all the assistance I can give on that point.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I thought that he had testified that there were two instances regarding goods and the second time he was not there. When he was referring to what he saw, that was the first delivery, and that was in May, or it may have been the picking up of the goods when he was not at home but his parents, because I can remember cross-examination talking about that and he said, "No, you can ask my mother".

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Because she was there at the time, yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Right, so that is the second time. The first time still I thought was in May.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: I think that that was cleared up by the reference to the conflict and it was clear that there was some confusion in this witness's mind as to, firstly, what the conflict consisted of. We talk of it as the three day shelling of Kozarac. He is talking about a much longer period of time. Secondly, the timing of it, because he is clearly saying it is after the shelling in Kozarac and after the police duties started. But, further than that I cannot take it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: How long did the conflict last? Was it still going on?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: The shelling lasted three days, but he appears to be referring to the whole time when these events were going on in Prijedor so he could be referring up to sometime in August or even later.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What was his relationship to Mr. Tadic or Mrs. Tadic once again?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: He was related but not closely. I think he was some kind of cousin, but there was not a close family relationship. The third point was the question of Radoslavka Lukic and her working hours. The cite for this is page 4567. I will quote directly from the question: Question: "What were your working hours?" This is from 20th June. "I worked from 7 o'clock to 3 o'clock for a while every day for some time, and subsequently there would be such shifts one whole day, one day off, and that is how we worked depending on the needs". Further question: "Did you work in other shifts too?" to which the answer is: "I did. For a while I worked from 7.00 to 3.00, then I worked the whole day or, rather, from 7 o'clock in the morning until the evening hours, that is, 8.00 or 9 o'clock". She then mentions the curfew.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is 4567?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does that indicate around that transcript cite when she started? Did she start on June 10th or June 20th?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: June 20th, and that is indicated on the same page.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: June 20th or thereafter?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That is right, yes. Your Honours, I want now to move on to the checkpoint books, the duty lists. The Defence has provided two pieces of very concrete evidence about Dusko Tadic's work in the traffic police. You will recall that the first (which are Exhibits 63 to 65) are the duty lists. These were filled in daily after the shifts had been worked and they were filled in by Zoran Cvijic who, for reasons we have heard, was not able to come and give evidence. In addition for this period, we have the checkpoint book, D66, also written by Zoran Cvijic. This is written the day before the shifts take place and in a different format from the duty lists. We could not persuade Zoran Cvijic to come and give evidence, but we did hear in rebuttal from Fikret Kadiric, a Prosecution witness, who confirmed that Zoran Cvijic even at his time was working in the administrative section of his department. We have also heard evidence from those who knew what Dusko Tadic's duties were, because they were with him in the traffic police. The first traffic policeman we heard was Miroslav Brdar who produced these books. He testified, as is borne out by the books, that he worked with Dusko Tadic and Miroslav Cvijic on all the shifts and how they never left the checkpoint during the shifts. We also heard evidence from Duro Prpos, Commander of the traffic police at the time, who supervised the work of Dusko Tadic and his colleagues. Duro Prpos was, in our view, an extremely important witness. We were very disappointed, as the Court is aware, that he could not come to The Hague to give evidence. He wish to do so. He was prevented from doing so, and it cannot be said in the light of that that his evidence is of any lesser value because it was given by video link. He confirmed that the duty lists were accurate, that they were kept according to a system and that he had supervised Zoran Cvijic who wrote the lists. He also gave evidence that, in his position as Commander, he would check the policemen on duty at irregular intervals, sometimes more than once during a shift, to ensure that everything was working properly and that everyone was at their post. I recall Judge Stephen asking him if they could be sure once he had checked that he would not return and he replied that, no, they could not and part of his duties was to make sure they never knew when he was coming. He also obtained and produced at the request of the Court the unredacted versions of these lists which we had been unsuccessful in securing. When these exhibits were produced in their unredacted versions, there was no flaw in their content. We suggest these are genuine working documents. They were in existence at the time of Fikret Kadiric and his own entry, indeed, is in the checkpoint book. We say that it is inconceivable that these two different types of written record are anything apart from what they purport to be. They are records made at the time showing hour by hour who was working where. They agree with each other. The Prosecution, in our submission, has produced no evidence undermining the accuracy of these records, although there has been some speculation on their accuracy. We suggest that the Defence in producing the witnesses who can speak to them has produced overwhelming evidence that they are, in fact, correct. For the second period when Dusko was in the Prijedor police, we also have records. We have heard from Mirko Vujanovic who compiled these records. They cover a period from the 7th August until 9th September when Dusko Tadic moved to the Kozarac police station. During this time Dusko Tadic was no longer working in the traffic police. He was working for the central police station in a security capacity. As with the very similar records from the traffic police, these are written up a day after the shift was worked. Mr. Vujanovic testified that each entry was written in his own hand and that it was taken from the daily schedules drawn up by the shift Commander. He testified that if a policeman had been absent from duty that would have been noted on the schedules, and he would not then have registered him in the book as being present. The Prosecution in their second cross-examination of this witness produced evidence intended to show that these books were unreliable. The first piece of evidence they produced were some patrol reports from the Kozarac police station which relate to the period at the beginning of September and which, to some degree, conflict with the hours in the duty stats. The witness when presented with these said that he had no knowledge of them. He did not know about the workings of the Kozarac police station. He did not even know who the Commander was. He knew nothing about what went on there. He simply could not comment beyond saying that he knew his own station, his own system, and he knew that his own books were accurate. So the situation we have is that we have these patrol reports. We have heard no evidence relating to them. As the Court is aware, we were unable to secure the attendance of witnesses from the Kozarac police station who could have testified on this matter, and who could have explained their provenance and talked about their reliability or lack of reliability. They are simply documents which stand on their own and, in assessing the comparative weight to be given to these and to the duty stats for whom we have had the compiler in Court explaining the system, explaining how it worked, this must be borne in mind. The second piece of evidence that the Prosecution produced was a daily schedule of the type that was referred to by Mr. Vujanovic from which he took the duty lists. This is the daily schedule which is dated 21st August, but which I think was established actually refers to 12th August. We established by looking at other names on the list and we found that everyone, including Dusko Tadic, tied up with the times on 12th August. This was mentioned yesterday by the Prosecution. The theory on it was that although this might have referred to 12th August, this gave some indication of the poverty of the system used and that, perhaps, all the reports were simply written up at the end of the month and these got shuffled somewhere at that stage. I would like to remind the Court that when Mr. Vujanovic gave evidence, having said that the date might have been transposed (and that had, in fact, been found out to be likely), he said (and this is page 5439) that the note at the top of the schedule which includes the date (and which I will read out to the Court) would not have been on the schedule at the time. The note says: "The following is page 5 of the daily schedule of shifts at the police station (1) for 21st August 1992 with a note that the daily schedules of the police employees were regular". It is signed and stamped. This is the piece of information which Mr. Vujanovic said would not have been on the list at the time. It appears, on the face of it, a very odd piece of information to be on a daily working document. It says that it is page 5 of the daily schedule. It is likely that a date, if there, would have perhaps been on page 1 of that schedule. This piece of material was not on the lists when Mr. Vujanovic wrote them out. It was put on at a date afterwards. He does not know when. It may be that it was for the purposes of this Court. The mistake that was made about the date must have been made at that stage and not at the earlier stage when the lists were being compiled. So I suggest that the confusion which the Prosecution said might have occurred could not have occurred. To talk briefly about the police records in general, it was suggested yesterday that even if they are not actually fabricated for the purpose, which I think is beyond question that they are not, it is very likely that they would be inaccurate, that they have a very questionable value. Firstly, I would suggest that for the fact we have two books, separate books, from the Orlovci checkpoint at least, containing the same information, suggests that they are not inaccurate. It is far less likely that two books would have the same inaccuracies than it is that one would be inaccurate. It is further suggested that even if they are not actually inaccurate, they have very little relevance because policemen could be posted to other places without this being noted. This is supposedly in part substantiated by the fact that the witness, Radoslavka Lukic, said there was a curfew after a certain time and so there would be no vehicles for them to check. I would have thought that if there was a curfew during some or all of this period, you would still need to man the checkpoints to ensure that the curfew was enforced. It is no good laying down a curfew and then sending all the police home. It is further said that the police were all engaged in cleansing activities anyway. It may be true that many of the regular police were engaged in these activities. There is no evidence that this is true on any large scale of the traffic police. If we look at the evidence that we have about members of the traffic police, Duro Prpos, we heard in rebuttal, that a witness had seen him at the SUP in Prijedor on a day when he was taken there with a bus load of other prisoners. We have heard that Zeljko Maric was seen when prisoners were being separated and taken to the camps. Mr. Reid told us that one of the names which appeared on the unredacted list -- I believe the name was Bosko Grabez -- was a person about whom statements had been made in connection with atrocities. What about the rest of these policemen? We have had no witness, including Mr. Reid, who perhaps we can assume would have told us about these things if he had read about them in statements since he told us about Bosko Grabez, who said that any other of these traffic policemen who are relevant to our case had been involved in these events. In particular, let us look at the two colleagues of Dusko Tadic, Miroslav Brdar, who came to the Court, Miroslav Cvijic. They have not been associated in this trial with any of the events in any way and they were the ones who saw Dusko Tadic day by day and worked with him day by day. What were they doing? Were they staying at their checkpoint and holding the fort while Dusko Tadic went off to the camps, or did they perhaps go along with him and nobody happened to see them there? Or is it more likely, in fact, that they were entirely unconnected with these atrocities and that is why we have heard nothing about them? They were unconnected with these atrocities, as was their colleague Dusko Tadic. That is all I intend to say on the police books, unless your Honours have any questions?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have one question and it relates to Mr. Prpos's testimony. As I recall, he testified that the first book was filled out by his deputy, and that he said it was done with some rhythm, one day on two days off.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that a mistake on his part?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: There is a rhythm to the shifts in that once one has --- what he said, I think, was that once had seen how the shifts work for a few days, one can carry on in the same pattern, because if someone is working say, 7.00 to 3.00 one day, then they will be on the 3.00 to 9.00 shift the next day and the 9.00 to 7.00 shift the following day, that is the sort of pattern that is followed. At some stage they then change to 12 hour shifts which they rotate, so that they have 12 hours on and 24 off. So there is some kind of pattern to it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But it is not the rhythm that he described, one day on, two days off?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That is not right, and I do not remember him saying it in those words, unless he was simply giving an illustration of how patterns occur. But since he had the books in front of him, I think it is unlikely that he would have got that wrong knowing that these books were in front of him, that he had just been looking through them and that they clearly did not say one day on, two days off, although there was a rhythm.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If he did say that, then what should I conclude from that, if he did say that?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: If he did say that, I would suggest he is using that as an example of the sort of rhythm that can be set up, the sort of method that can be set up, but not the method that was actually used there.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. I do not have the transcript cite and it is just something that I recall actually from my notes. The other question relates to the uniforms or the uniform that Mr. Tadic wore. Mrs. Tadic testified that he came home on 16th wearing his blue uniform.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Police uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, and Mr. Brdar or officer Brdar testified that he wore, as I recall, the uniform from before the war, light grey uniform, he, Mr. Brdar, and Mr. Tadic wore a camouflage uniform. Let me see if I can remember the concerns that I had. Mr. Maric also testified that the policemen at the checkpoint wore grey uniforms before June or July, and after that they got camouflage uniforms. The gentleman who was delivering food for the 43rd Brigade testified that he saw Mr. Tadic in a blue uniform. I thought Mr. Tadic testified that he typically wore a camouflage uniform, unless his other was in the cleaners. What should I try to draw from these uniforms, if anything? Just people were mistaken or what? You tell me, if it is as I suggest it is.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic's evidence was that he had a camouflage type of uniform given to him by his brother ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand ----

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: --- and that he only had one police uniform. I think it was the other way round, that he wore the police uniform when he could and when it needed to be laundered he would wear the camouflage uniform. There are different types of police uniform, police camouflage and the plain police uniform. I think his evidence was that he was wearing the plain police uniform or his brother's camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What about, if I am correct, about Mr. Brdar? I may have that backwards too. If he testified that Mr. Tadic testified wore a camouflage but he wore a light grey, and if Mr. Maric testified that they wore light grey until June or July and then they got camouflage, what do I do with that? Do I accept their testimony?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: What I would say is that they each remembered one of the uniforms that Tadic wore rather than both of them, rather than the fact that he had two different ones. It is likely, I suppose, after this time that a witness may not remember that he had seen Dusko Tadic in two different uniforms, but only called to mind one of the ones that he had seen him in.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, it does. I can assume that they just did not recall. But, I mean, I heard Mr. Kay talk at length about statements where a person said one thing and they did not say the second thing so, therefore, you can assume, you know, that maybe they were lacking in candour.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: I would think that this is not a problem of candour but merely of recollection, that there is evidence that he had both of these uniforms and these witnesses, well, Mr. Brdar would have seen him in both and Mr. Maric might not have seen him in both, or had simply forgotten that he had the second one. I would not think that there is a problem about their honesty on that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Maric testified that he worked with him but most often he said they were on different shifts.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In fact, he never worked with him if you look at this spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That is right. I think he was wrong on that, that it was just the takeover of shifts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Before you leave, can I ask you two questions? The first one is, is there any evidence at all about traffic police on duty at checkpoints anywhere going off on so-called higher duties?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: There is no evidence in this trial of that happening at all. I stand corrected if I have missed something.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Except for Maric, if you accept the Prosecution's and Mrs. Klipic's testimony?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That is right. There has been that suggestion that he was sorting out people, but this may not have been while he was doing traffic duties, we do not know, because that was considerably earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Is there any explanation in the evidence of why you had three grown men undertaking the day in, day out, the checkpoint duty?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: There is no evidence on that and I think the question was not asked. I can merely speculate that it was felt that there was a dangerous situation in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But there is no evidence about it?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: There is no evidence. The question was not put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I thought that the three police officers would check licences and look for weapons, was it, or was it, and then the two military, normally there were two military also, so there were five people ----

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That is right because they dealt with military vehicles and the traffic police dealt with civilian vehicles.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But there did not appear to be a lot of traffic. I heard each of the witnesses who served at the checkpoint say they never saw the transporting of detainees or bus loads of people. I also wonder what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: It may be that there was less traffic at the time, but that it was potentially of a more dangerous nature in a conflict situation, but I can only speculate because this was not actually in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are going to move to another area?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Yes. I am now going to move on to the hours between these police duties. We have accounted for the hours in the book. What about the time when he was not on duty? We have heard evidence from Mira Tadic that during that time he lived in the apartment at Pecani after they had moved into it on 27th. We have heard evidence, importantly, from Mr. Brdar who said (and the cite for this is page 4469) when policemen were on duty they had to be at home or at least contactable in case they were needed in an emergency. They were not allowed to travel around without permission. We have heard evidence from Nada Vlacina who visited the family in Pecani regularly. She also lived in Pecani, a near neighbour of theirs, and also of Witness D who said she saw him several times a week in Prijedor during this period. Jelena Gajic saw him often after about mid June in Prijedor. There is also evidence such as the visits of Ljubo Tadic to the family in Pecani. The Prosecution’s witnesses, Adil and Nasiha Jakupovic, saw him in Prijedor on occasions when he was not on duty. We have several sources of information from people, particularly Nada Vlacina, Witness D, normal women who had no connection with events, no reason to lie about this. Naturally, they cannot testify to every minute that he was not on duty. It would be unnatural if they could. That can only be done by his close family, and that is what Mira Tadic says. So we would suggest that the evidence that Dusko was working in the police, was living in Prijedor during this period, is very strong evidence and, in particular, that his recorded hours of work are a substantial counter to the allegations that have been made regarding this period. I am going to move on to events after September 9th when Dusko Tadic moved to Kozarac to begin his work there. We have heard that he worked part-time for the police there until 19th November. We have heard evidence from Dusan Vajagic and Witness Y who were his colleagues there. But we have also heard that during the autumn of that year he was increasingly engaged in works in the locality, in particular, in the Local Commune of which he was Secretary. We have heard evidence from Witness A, from Stojan Smoljic, as to the work he did there bringing back life to Kozarac. He also became President of the Kozarac branch of the SDS. These two jobs, Secretary of the Local Commune, President of the SDS, are closely linked to each other. These two institutions are working hand-in-hand. They are housed in the same premises, and it appears that in both the Party and the Local Commune the priority in this locality is the reconstruction of Kozarac as a viable place to live.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I ask you a question? Did Mr. Tadic work as a police officer until November 19th?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: November 19th, I think, is the date that he gave as the end of his police duties in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So then from September 9th through November 19th he would have a regular assignment as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That is right, but the work was part-time rather than full-time.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What do you mean by that? That was really my question.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: We do not have evidence, your Honour, in this court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do we not have spreadsheets?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Not for Kozarac, only for Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, so we do not have.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: But we do know that he was very much engaged in the work of the Local Commune and SDS and that as the year went on this took up more and more of his time.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Did the gentleman Y, I think, not testify that he worked with him as a police officer until November?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That is right, and Dusan Vajagic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Not full-time, you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Not full-time in that he was also doing all this other work as well.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: How can we determine then how much time he did for both?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: We only have the evidence of witnesses. We do not have documentary evidence with regard to this. We were not able to get Goran Babic, his Commander, to come and give evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Dasic, was it -- who is the gentleman in charge? He testified that from October until December Mr. Tadic left Prijedor with him in the morning and then spend the day inventorying housing, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That is right, your Honour. That was a sort of commission of three people which sometime in October was started up.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Until December 1st or 2nd?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Again some date in December.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Was it his testimony that Mr. Tadic would leave with him from Prijedor 8.30 in the morning usually, 8.00 or 8.30.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: It was not every day. It was not every day, but when they did work that was the sort of hours that they would work. That is as I recall his testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I was thinking that it was every day because Judge Stephen, I think, asked if he had some records. Of course, that does not mean that it is every day that he worked. Mr. Smoljic, what was his testimony regarding Mr. Tadic? Do you remember him? He testified via video.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That is right, your Honour. He was the witness who had moved as a refugee to Kozarac on October 27th, if I recall it rightly, with his family. He said that Dusko Tadic had helped him to find somewhere to live and that Dusko Tadic had helped him by giving him some work in the Local Commune. He talked about Dusko Tadic's work in the Local Commune. So, President of the SDS, Secretary of the Local Commune, and both these institutions being very closely linked. Indeed, we have heard from Jozo Popovic, a refugee from Velika Kladusa, who succeeded him in both positions so that the position of Secretary of the Local Commune and President of the SDS is still in the same hands. We have heard what kind of work these jobs involved. The Prosecution case is that Dusko Tadic was heavily politically involved during this time. If we look to what Jozo Popovic says on this, he agrees that the SDS was a political party but he gives no evidence of it engaging in any political as opposed to practical activity. I quote at transcript cite 5459: "The SDS is a political party which means that it is engaged in political activity". Then he says: "Within that scope it proposed certain personnel solutions for the Local Commune. It assessed the political situation and through its representatives in the executive bodies of the Local Commune it would implement that policy". He goes on to talk about the implementation of that policy, and this involves the examples he gives, such things as accommodating people, setting up education and health services, organising supplies of water and electricity and giving humanitarian aid. These are not heavily political activities to be involved in. This is why I say that the two institutions are very closely linked. What they are both doing is, in fact, bringing help to Kozarac. We have also heard evidence from Witness Y, also a refugee. He was a member of the local board of the SDS. He told the Court he was not interested in politics. He had only become a member of the SDS in August 1992. He said that Dusko Tadic did not make political speeches. He said at page 4700: "All we were interested in was work, nothing else. All we wanted to do was to bring life back to the Local Commune of Kozarac". Again, practical, not ideological. He said as the reason that Dusko Tadic was chosen for these positions was "because I did not know these people. He knew everyone from before so he was most suitable to deal with them, to have all the right contacts. He knew the people, knew the area and that is why he was elected as chairman". That is at page 4703. There was some attempt in cross-examination to make Witness Y say that Dusko Tadic was very closely connected with the SDS in Prijedor. These attempts were unsuccessful and he simply repeated that they needed someone as President who was familiar with the area. We also heard evidence from Dusan Vajagic who has been mentioned earlier today, also a refugee from Velika Kladusa, also joined the SDS for the first time when he got to the area. Indeed, he became the Secretary of the SDS some month after he arrived. This gives some counter to the suggestion that these posts were handed out to people who had been active in the conflict in the area.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What was his name again?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Dusan V-A-J-A-G-I-C. He was the rather tall and thin man with glasses.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That was the man that I was remembering, but I do not see the name. That is what I am looking for. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: He gave evidence right next to Witness Y on the list, if that is of assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I am sorry. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: He said at page 4723: "I joined the SDS so that I could help the population who had moved there in the first place, to have a contact with Prijedor, because somebody had to represent that population or ask for something on behalf of the population in Kozarac". Again he talks about SDS meetings, building the local community. Of course, there was contact with these organisations and authorities in Prijedor, but there is nothing sinister in that connection. There was no money in Kozarac. The only help that they could get was from Prijedor. So the fact that they had to have contact with Prijedor, to ask them for aid, does not automatically show that this was an organ which was in the hands of the Prijedor authorities. Indeed, we have heard much evidence that Prijedor was very resistant to the whole aims of rebuilding Kozarac. So we have three witnesses here, two of them achieved positions in the SDS, one in the Local Commune, who do not fit with the Prosecution profile of people who were given such jobs, that is, people who have been active in the conflict and are being rewarded for their activity. The Prosecution have said only a person who was absolutely loyal to the Serb people could have held such positions. I put before you in that context Dusan Vajagic who had only joined the SDS in August 1992 and was almost immediately made Secretary. These three witnesses, we submit, are ordinary people. They are refugees. Certainly, Dusan Vajagic and Witness Y took no interest in politics. Their only reason for being in the SDS was that they wanted to rebuild Kozarac which has constantly been asserted.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vajagic, was he not an officer in the SDS in Velika Kladusa before he came? That is a different person.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That was Mr. Popovic, your Honour, whom I mentioned first.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But he was an officer of the SDS, President, was it?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That is right, in Vela Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then he came to Kozarac in August or os?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That is right, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Apart from these refugees, do we have any information about how many people were living in the unfortunate town of Kozarac at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: I do not know that we do. I cannot think of it offhand. There have been certain ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I mean, the pictures make it look like utterly desolate.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That is right. There are some surrounding areas included in this and, in fact, these refugees did not actually live in Kozarac proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Many of the villages around are less devastated than the centre of Kozarac which you have seen so many pictures of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose that is it, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: We have spoken already of the commission recording the deserted houses, heard extensive evidence from Mr. Dasic on this. We have heard that Dusko Tadic was not even head of this commission reviewing properties, this three-person commission. So where is all this power that is supposedly invested in him? Again during this time he has remained living in Prijedor. The same witnesses have said they continued to see him. Mr. Dasic has said, as your Honour pointed out, that he was taken from Prijedor to Kozarac. Mr. Smoljic gave evidence that he saw Dusko Tadic arriving by bus from Prijedor. Again, it has been made clear to the Court by both those witnesses as well as others that he had no means of transport at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Did Mrs. Tadic testify that he took the bus also and would come back either by bus or hitch a ride, come back with Babic, rather, or hitch a ride.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: I think that she did, although I cannot give you the cite for it, but I think that is what she said. Certainly the transport situation was talked of. I forget her exact answer on how he travelled, but it was certainly made clear that he had no car.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Did she mention Mr. Dasic or did she say he travelled by bus?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: I do not recall her mentioning Mr. Dasic in evidence. That covers the period in question. Just a few more words on the two members of his family who covered so much of this period. Firstly, his wife, Mira Tadic, who was with him throughout this time has confirmed the details of his alibi; his brother Ljubo who has given evidence relating particularly to those days in Banja Luka before he returned to Kozarac when the two Tadic brothers were constantly in each other's company. It is easy to say that because these two witnesses are so close to the defendant they would, of course, support his alibi, and their evidence is in some way tarnished by this relationship with the defendant. It is a difficulty for the Defence that in many cases of alibi the person that the defendant spends the most time with is a member of his family. This suggestion by the Prosecution is a very easy one to make in any of these kinds of cases, but I would suggest that after cross-examination of these witnesses their evidence has remained largely intact, and that their evidence should be seen for what it is, strong evidence supporting Dusko Tadic's case. Of course, they have a great interest in supporting him, no one could possibly deny that. It would be unnatural if they did not have that interest. But while the fact that they are such close members of his family must be taken into account, we suggest that it cannot alone show in any way that they have been lying in the evidence that they gave before this Court. All this evidence is a strong support for Dusko Tadic's alibi, for his assertion that he did not commit the crimes during this period, that he was involved in a large number of other activities which consumed his time and his energy, and that even had he had the means of transport, which he did not, to roam around the countryside, go to Omarska, go to the camps, he was, in fact, living, working and occupied elsewhere when these crimes were committed. I would like to turn finally to the letters and interviews which Dusko Tadic made earlier before he gave evidence. We have heard a bit from the Prosecution about the contradictions between what he said previously and what he says now.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me. Before you go into that subject, how much additional time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff and Mr. Orie, tell me again how much time you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I need approximately half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have been shortening while listening -- I have limited it down to three quarters of an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If we go until 6.30 will you be able to complete? That will be an hour and 15 minutes? Half hour, you said 20 minutes, that is less than an hour.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: But there is the half hour, the 20 minutes and the three-quarters of an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What does that add up to? The interpreters can add it up real well! An hour and a half. Can we finish in an hour and a half?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: We could try.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can we go -- you cannot go?

utterances.speaker: MISS FEATHERSTONE
utterances.text: They are saying until 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have to make phone calls since my children are waiting to celebrate my birthday that was last Saturday. I will do this.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Tell them to come over here and we will all celebrate together. Happy birthday. 6 o'clock. If we go to 6.00, I do not know whether we are going to finish tomorrow. Let us do what we can. I do not want to rush you, but I do not know when we will have time to finish this. Tomorrow we will be adjourning at 1.00. Friday afternoon is the only time.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: I will be as brief as I can. I hope to finish by 5.30.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, I do not want to rush you. No, take your time, take your time. We have spent months so let us not rush it. I am just telling you the schedule. We need to adjourn at 1.00. We will not be here on Thursday. We cannot use the courtroom on Friday morning. When can we begin to use it on Friday?

utterances.speaker: MISS FEATHERSTONE
utterances.text: Probably about noon.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Noon, perhaps noon.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So that is the schedule. You may go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just talking about the allegations that Dusko Tadic has made many contradictory statements about his movements during this time. I suggest to the Court that when they read the interviews and the letters at their leisure, that what is in fact striking is not the minor deviations which could be expected in this kind of covering of six months, but the overall broad consistency of what he said not only from the German interviews onwards but right back as far as his work report written in 1993, long before he could have known that he was going to need to produce this kind of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I was going to ask you in any event what comments you had to make on the work report. I would like to hear you on that and I would like to suggest that it is not really right, is it, to say that at the time that he prepared the work report, which was in the second half of '93, he already had been interviewed by the woman who made the German film, had he not?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: He had not been interviewed by her, although she had made a film and taken shots of him at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Allegations had been made in the film about him.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: What I suppose I am saying is he could not have possibly have known that he was going to be arrested in connection with anything that had gone on at this time. Nobody else from the area had been threatened or arrested and, as it happens, none of them have to this date. He could not have known at that time what was going to happen in Munich, although it is true that he may have had some knowledge of the allegations made against him. If I may I will deal with that last, because I think that is how it fits in the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: So our suggestion is that it is not the defendant who has tailored his story to fit the evidence available as it comes in. This is a defendant who, right from the beginning, has wanted to speak, has been eager to speak, eager to clear his name, has requested that people interview him. It is of course a daunting task to recollect six months worth of dates and times, and I would suggest that no one could do it with absolute accuracy. What he has done is piece together his movements over that period as accurately as possible, and evidence has come up which has enabled him to be more accurate. So, for example, when we got the duty stats, the police reports, confirming he started work on 16th June rather than 17th June that was something that he was then able to say, "That is right, I did get the date wrong." We would suggest that that is not a defendant tailoring his evidence. It is quite understandable that one gets a date slightly wrong and then, when presented with documentary evidence, can correct that. From the start the story has been the same. We have the family leaving Kozarac in April and May mentioned in the work report, in the first Prosecution interview, in the way it was told in evidence. The same names in the Prosecution interview are mentioned: Trivo Reljic, Jelena Gajic. We have Dusko Tadic's escape from Kozarac, 23rd May. Work report, he says, "One day before fighting I left for Banja Luka", so on with the German interview, both Prosecution interviews and in evidence. In all his three interviews, and I refer to one German and two Prosecution interviews, he speaks of visiting Kozarac to his family house. He is hazy about the times which this has happened. He has cleared this up in evidence. We suggest there is nothing sinister about that. These are not dates on which major allegations are made. He has not tailored his evidence to fit the dates of indicted incidents. There is no indicted incident in these early days of June. It is simply that, over time, his recollection has become clearer as to what his movements were. The start of his work in Prijedor I have already alluded to. He started, he says, on 17th June in many of his interviews. Only in evidence does he say it was 16th June. I would like to remind the Court that, despite what the Prosecution has said, we did not have the duty stats at the time that he last was interviewed by the Prosecution. We had simply the letter from Simo Drljaca which was written on a single sheet of paper listing his apparent duties. It appears from the transcript of the interview that at the time he was asked about it, Dusko Tadic was not actually looking at the letter. In any case, he said in evidence that he had scant regard for this document and, knowing what we do about the person who signed it, I think that we can understand that he may have felt that this was not a proper official document or one to which he could attach great weight. We have heard from the Prosecution about the different things he said when he arrived in Banja Luka: where he stayed, who he was with. He has said throughout in all three interviews that he spent either the first or the first two nights with Radovan Vokic, scarcely a substantial difference. He spent the next nights with Martin and Mileva Dzaja when he was not in Banja Luka. They are not clear about the dates when he was in Banja Luka. There may be some lack of clarity. The broad picture remains the same. We have heard in his German interview and his first Prosecution interview him say he went to Trnopolje camp, five times he says in his German interview, four in his Prosecution interview. Right from the beginning in Germany he admits he went to that camp five times. There is no attempt to avoid this even from the beginning. Each time he has named the time that he went with Jovo Samardzija. He could not possibly have known that Jovo Samardzija would come and give evidence to that unless it was true. We have talked early today about the uniforms again. He talks about them in all three interviews. In each one we hear about the camouflage clothes given by Ljubo. He says in his German interview: "I did not own a camouflage uniform." This does not necessarily exclude those clothes. We have heard in evidence he did not consider it proper uniform. They were simply clothes that you wore over your ordinary clothes. He talks as well of the police uniforms that he wore. We have heard about the two uniforms or the one uniform from Milan Kusota. They were given in a bundle with the rifle. Well, whether there was one or two I would suggest is irrelevant. The defendant has said that he never wore them. They were too small for him. He never used them. He may have forgotten there were two, there was one. I suggest it does not matter. We have the weapons, in particular the rifle certificate. In each interview he said that he had had the same weapon, the automatic rifle and the pistol. The rifle certificate was discussed in the German interview. His answer to the question about it was: "I did not receive any weapons from the staff of the Territorial Defence." Dusko Tadic says that the certificate was not shown to him at that time. The statement that he was making was true. On the evidence now he did not receive weapons from the staff of the Territorial Defence. The Prosecution have produced a witness, whose name I forget, to say that he was at the interview and there was some question with him about whether documents had been produced. His answer was, "They were always produced", but he was not specific about this case.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Tadic actually testify that that certificate had not been shown to him?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That that certificate had?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Had not been shown to him.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That is what he said, yes. He said in the German interview it was not shown to him.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He said that in the German interview or did he say it in court when referring to the certificate that it was not shown to him?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: I have not actually got it down. I know he said it either in a later interview or in evidence that it was not shown to him at the time. My recollection is that he said it in evidence. I may be wrong on that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You can move ahead and look for the citation.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: I will find you the cite on that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I did not think it was that clear. I thought I had asked Mr. Tieger that question, and then they produced the German officer who said it was shown to him. I do not remember one way or the other because it was not clear to me, that is why I had asked him.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: All I can say I recall is the discussion coming up, whether it was in evidence or in other interview I cannot recall, but I shall look that up. Then we have the question of where the certificate comes from. He said he had two certificates, one from Slobodan Bokan in Prijedor and the one we have in court which is from his brother Ljubo Tadic. It is clear that the one we have in court cannot come from Prijedor because it says at the top: "Territorial Defence, Banja Luka". So, I suggest that when he was shown the original certificate he took it to be something that it was not, a document that he had got from Prijedor. He did not read it carefully or he could not have said that it came from Prijedor when it very clearly said "Banja Luka". He then said in evidence that he got it from Ljubo and filled it out himself, and that it was a separate one that he had got from Prijedor. He gets some details wrong. He gets some dates wrong. Who would not? Dusko Tadic in evidence, and I quote at page 6137: "I may be wrong about the dates, that is true, I may be wrong about some description, whether a sleeve was blue or whether a uniform was blue or yellow, but I know where I was all my life. I cannot forget that and I cannot be wrong about whether I was in some location where I had never been in my life." If I now turn finally to the work report, there was a lot of discussion about this document. There was a list of people it was to be sent to, including President Karadzic. It was apparently not sent to him or any of the other people on the list, apart from being given to the authorities in Prijedor. We have had a lot of quotes from that document put to the defendant. We have heard a lot about what he said about other people, what he said about the authorities. Our suggestion about this is that it is a rather pathetic document. It is self-aggrandizing, it makes this defendant out to be important, and it shows a great degree of self-importance in the document. We must recall the context in which the document was written. At this stage Dusko Tadic felt that he was being hounded out of Prijedor. He had been arrested or had attempts to arrest him several times. He had been sent to the front at Gradacac. He was having enormous problems with the authorities who clearly did not want him around. He saw himself as being someone who had been wronged, and he gives this long list of grievances against all the persons who wronged him. We suggest that the main point of the document is not that, that that can be explained by his situation at the time and, think what you might of it, it does not make him a war criminal whatever it says about his feelings and his character at that time. We suggest the main point of it is what it says about where he was during these events in Prijedor. Now this is a document intended for those in authority in Republika Srpska, including President Karadzic, at least at the time that he wrote it, even if it was never sent. It is not sent to people who would find much to condemn had he said, "I have taken part in these events". On the contrary, even if he were not going to say, and it would be, we concede, unusual to say that he had actually committed atrocious acts in the camps, it would surely have helped his cause to say that he had taken part in what the people he wrote it to clearly saw to be a commendable conflict. He was being sent to the front to join the war effort. On the Prosecution evidence he had done a great deal for the war effort already. Why did he not say that? Even if he was not going to talk about significant events, which the Prosecution have alleged, why did he not say that he helped with the fighting in Kozarac? Why did he not say that he helped in the camps? We suggest the reason that he did not say this was because it is the truth, that he was not there. He is not at this stage providing an alibi for himself. He is providing a true account of those events. The quote that I would read to you from it which, we suggest, is the significant part of that letter, is on pages 7 to 8 of that report in which he says: "Fighting in Kozarac started on 25th May 1992. One day before that I had left for Banja Luka where my family lived as refugees in an abandoned house living off our last savings. I never took part in the attack on Kozarac because, despite everything, when I had been living among these people for 35 years I still did not see why I should have to shoot at my former neighbours when surely things would change with time, because truth will out and because I did not see why all that had to end with destruction and devastation in setting up camps and looting other people's property disregarding who the previous owner was."

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does it say in that work report that the fighting started on 25th and he had left the day before?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: It does, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That is what makes it so important, in my view, to know to what extent, if any, the accused was at that time of writing aware of allegations that he had committed war crimes, so that it might be said that he was, in effect, writing that in the light of those sorts of allegations and very carefully avoiding any suggestion that he had done what he had done?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: I do not recall whether he was asked in evidence whether he knew about the allegations at the time. I also do not recall the date of the Monika Gras film. I do not know if I can get assistance from the other side of the room there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I think we know that that was early in '93. There was also, I think, some evidence from the accused of sitting in a cafe in Banja Luka and joking with a friend over ridiculous allegations of war crimes by Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That was evidence not by the accused but by Nikola Petrovic who said he had been ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: He had been with the accused?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: That is right, and the accused was not asked about that in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Also someone testified that an article had appeared in the Zagreb paper, I do not think a date was given though, regarding Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That was the article that they were joking about.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, that is the one. I think the context in which it was put was that they were saying how ridiculous it was that these allegations were being made. There is then some evidence that he knew something about these things at the time. No evidence that he was in any fear that anything would be done about any of the events in Republika Srpska, let alone to him in Prijedor. That is all I have to say, unless there are further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: There is just one transcript cite. On page 6124 of Dusko Tadic's evidence he talked of the document, the rifle certificate, and he says: "I did not see that document in Munich during the interview", and it carries on after that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Orie?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, we will adjourn tonight at 6.00, but you take your time. We have tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I will address to you the issue of the character of the conflict internal or international. The Appeals Chamber has given us some guidance regarding the character of the conflict. On the question of the existence of an armed conflict as such, a clear answer has been given by the Appeals Chamber. Both the intensity requirement and the relationship requirement were met in the Prijedor region in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the summer of 1992; pages 37 and 38 of the decision of the Appeals Chamber. This of course is a global assessment, and does not say anything about a nexus between the alleged specific acts of the accused and the conflict. The Prosecution and the Defence seem to agree that it will be necessary to establish such a nexus as well in order to reach the decision that Mr. Tadic would be guilty. Unfortunately, I am not capable in explaining to you anything about whether any acts were committed for pleasure or for whatever other reason. I am only asking you to look at this very cautiously. You will understand that I cannot give you any help on that because my client was not there. So, what was in his mind at that moment I cannot explain to you. Of course, the Appeals Chamber did not hear any evidence of fact necessary to establish such a nexus. It only demonstrates that the ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think the transcript has stopped. No, it has not. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Once again, your Honour, the decision of the Appeals Chamber only demonstrates that the events in the Prijedor area were not separated in time or geographically from the armed conflict that existed at that time in Bosnia and Herzegovina. But then the main question that still needs to be answered is whether the acts of the indictment took place in the context of an international armed conflict. I will very much concentrate on what I consider to be the relevant time, that is on from mid-May, and I will especially pay a lot of attention to what happened after 19th May, the date of the withdrawal, the announced withdrawal, of the JNA. I will pay no attention to the applicability of international humanitarian law under the agreements of the conflicting parties, since the Appeals Chamber correctly indicated that the defendant has not been charged with any acts committed in violation of such agreements. I quote the Appeals Chamber: "To the extent that the conflict in which the alleged crimes were committed have been limited to clashes between Bosnian government forces and Bosnian rebel forces, they have been of an internal character, unless direct involvement of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia could be proven." That means, your Honours, that it would have to be established that the Bosnian Serbs were acting not as a rebellious entity, but as organs or agents of another state, again the wording of the Appeals Chamber. They were not. Apart from the absurd outcome placing the Bosnian Serbs at a substantial disadvantage vis-a-vis the central authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I submit that the evidence presented by the Prosecution does not justify the conclusion that the Bosnian Serbs were acting as organs or agents of the Federal Republic. As you may remember, in the early stages of the procedure we had the authority of Mr. Fenrick at that time saying that the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina was of an internal character on from 19th May. He later changed his mind because he had new information, as he told us, but it was never explained to us what the old information was and what had been added since then.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Was that not when he was with the Commission of Experts and now that he is wearing his Prosecution hat maybe that is ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If that is the only additional information, your Honour, I would not say that it is very relevant for us.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: As I recall it, it is a long time ago but as I recall it, that was when he was with the Commission of Experts, not that that makes any difference I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree but he never gave us any reason what he more afterwards when he changed his mind. We also of course have the authority of the International Red Cross, and we see that the Appeals Chamber is paying a lot of weight to it. Also the International Red Cross at that time came to the conclusion that it was an internal conflict. The Prosecution has presented evidence that the split up of the JNA has resulted in a very confusing situation, but of course it is no surprise to the Defence that there was no time at that moment available to order the issuing of entirely new uniforms. Of course, it would not be possible at that moment to search for new suppliers abroad, other than those already contracted in earlier days. If one manages what that would have meant under these circumstances, it is quite obvious that the Bosnian Serbs would use the channels they were used to, and that they were using the uniforms and equipment that were left behind. Quite some officers of the former JNA became officers in the VRS, the new army of the Serbian Republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am sorry, can I interrupt you for a moment just to see if I understand where you are going? Am I right in thinking that the Appeals Chamber concluded that there was an international armed conflict created by the invasion of Croatia and of Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: When I just was quoting the Appeals Chamber I think it was only on the part of the clashes between the Bosnian government forces and Bosnian rebel forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Did they not say there was both an international conflict and also an internal conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Well, they say that to make this part of the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina an international conflict we first would need proof of a direct involvement of the federal government in Belgrade. They were very specific on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, surely, but what I am trying to see is what your response is to this. My understanding is that it has been said certainly there was an international conflict. They also, I think, said that international conflicts extend to the totality of the countries in question. Then they say, but the particular conflict here may have been internal and not international. What do you say to the coexistence within the one territory of an international conflict and an internal conflict? Does one absorb the other? Is there a merger?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I think it depends. I do not think it ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Or can you have the two coexisting?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I think you can have the two coexisting but not at the same place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It must be in the same place because the international extends over the totality of the territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I can imagine that, for example, there is still some combat going on in one part of the country with a foreign neighbour, and in another part of the country you have an internal conflict. But as we pointed out already, and I think the Prosecution did more or less the same, the decision of the Appeals Chamber in this respect is rather confusing. I think we both expressed that. But specifically on this part of the conflict the Appeals Chamber says to make this an international conflict, and they are also drawing consequences out of that, I just told you that they would say that if it would have been an international conflict, clashes within Bosnia and Herzegovina between rebellious forces and the central government forces, that this would lead to an absurd outcome. That indicates, I think, what they feel about this aspect.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, the Defence filed a motion to dismiss the Article 2 allegations in the indictment, contending that Article 2 applies only if there is an international conflict and there was not one. The Appeals Chamber denies the motion to dismiss, do they not? They uphold the Trial Chamber's denial. So, how can the Appeals Chamber uphold the denial of a motion to dismiss when it should have been dismissed if it was not an international conflict ongoing?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that if the Appeals Chamber indicates that still some facts would have to be established before you finally can come to the conclusion whether this was an international conflict or not, they could not possible at that moment already decide that the motion would be granted.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So perhaps what they are doing is looking at the indictment and kind of treating it like a motion to dismiss in my system, that is, assuming that all of the allegations are true, then it would be an international conflict or no, without finding finally that it is an international conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: One of the allegations is ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Finding that if the Prosecutor proves what it alleges, then it would be an international conflict, but they have not gone so far as to say it has been proven.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: One of the allegations is that it all happened in an international conflict, so that still has to be proven. I think that is what the Appeals Chamber indicates, that at least quite some facts still have to be established before you can finally reach the conclusion whether these acts were committed at that time in an international conflict. Your Honours, it has become clear that the state of confusion I just referred to still influences the wording used by several experts and witnesses. If, for example, Mr. Tihic tells the Court that JNA soldiers used to wear the uniforms that we all knew from the previous JNA, that is page 8976 (?), it is clear that he refers to some kind of new JNA different from that of the previous JNA, and that is in fact the VRS, but he still calls them JNA soldiers. I will give you later another example of using the word "JNA", Dr. Gow used that word, when it actually means the remaining part of the JNA, then the VRS, on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The JNA had been a federal army of a Federal Republic. There is no legal reason to assume that only the Belgrade government was exclusively entitled to take possession of all the equipment, and to keep in command of all the officers and soldiers of the federal army. Bosnia-Herzegovina, and especially, I must admit that, the Bosnian Serbs, were taking part in the organisation and the operations of the JNA until the withdrawal of the JNA was ordered. The central government in Sarajevo did also claim the full control of any remainder of the JNA on their territory, as Dr. Gow testified in cross-examination. They would not accept anything less, however, than full control. Although the constitutional system had collapsed in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I refer to the lengthy statements of Professor Hayden, already in 1991 and although it was clear that the Bosnian Serbs were not participating in the new constitutional order and would not do so either, having established their own Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, after having held their own plebiscite, the central government was still claiming full control of all forces on Bosnia and Herzegovina territory. The Serbian Republic tried on its part to take control over the JNA materiel and people that were left behind in those areas where there was a Bosnian-Serb majority. Much attention has been paid to the comparison between the withdrawal of JNA of Croatia and the withdrawal of the JNA of Bosnia. One would easily overlook, however, the differences of the situation. Croatia had sought its dependence as a state of Croatians. The amendments of the constitution of Croatia had already illustrated the prominent place of the Croatian people in that state prior to its independence. It was therefore that the JNA only left equipment there where there was no Croat majority. Bosnia and Herzegovina, however, was a multi-ethnic state. Serbs were a constituent part of the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina, representing one third of the people. It is easily understood that the Belgrade government was not very much inclined to facilitate the Croatians, who were their enemies at that time, in providing them with equipment, although it might have been fair from a federal point of view to do so. In Bosnia and Herzegovina the Serbian population was the same ethnic origin. I think it hardly can be denied that there may have been common aspirations among Serbs, whether living in Serbia proper or in the Serbian majority part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So, they were of the same ethnic origin as the majority of the population of what would become the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Therefore, there was no reason for the Belgrade government whatsoever to frustrate the aspirations of the Bosnian Serbs. The central government of Bosnia and Herzegovina would not accept, however, anything else than full 100 per cent control of the JNA remainders, which they did not achieve to obtain. Many posts in the JNA in Bosnia and Herzegovina were held by Bosnian Serbs. Non-Bosnian Serbs that were holding posts like officers could decide whether they would return to the territory of the federation or would stay in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Most of them perhaps stayed. Non-Bosnian Serbs were already a minority in those parts of the JNA that were found on Bosnia and Herzegovina territory. For often very personal reasons a number of Serbs, not of Bosnian origin, decided to stay. I refer to the testimony given by Colonel Selak, page 1257. Although financial support from Belgrade does not alter the conflict, the internal conflict in an international one, I will spend a few words on this financial support. As Colonel Selak has testified on page 1274, the officers of the former JNA were still paid by Belgrade after 19th May 1992. I am not talking about pension, because I think it is self-explanatory that a former employer is under an obligation to pay these pensions independent of any subsequent new function the former employee has taken. First of all, one should take into account that the administrative system could not easily be changed under the circumstances of 1992. That would be a major operation in itself even under peaceful circumstances, but even if these payments would indicate a financial support for the Bosnian Serbs, this would not make the Bosnian Serbs organs or agents of the federal government in Belgrade. Just to give you an example, the Dutch government has paid for many, many years the salaries of those officers in the new Surinam Army, which was former colony of the Netherlands, those salaries of those officers who used to serve in the Dutch army before the independence of that colony. This does not make the Surinam Army an organ or agent of the Dutch government. The financial support of the United States government may have played even a decisive role in the Nicaraguan conflict. This, however, did not make the Contras agents or organs of the US government.
